title: Agent context engineering for production
description: Scalable agents need more than a good system prompt. Every LLM turn is a compiled view across session context, memory, artifacts, tool responses, examples, and instructions. This session covers context engineering: the discipline of providing exactly the right information at the right time. Covers context rot, skills vs. tools, session compaction, and the Vertex AI Memory Bank service with a live demo. Concludes with an AT&T production case study showing cross-channel, multi-session persistent memory.

segments.heading: From models to agents: why context engineering matters
segments.text: LLMs are inherently stateless: they generate text but cannot access real-time information, read a database, or plan multi-step tasks. Every agentic technique exists to overcome one or more of these limitations. Large context windows create the illusion that more context is always better, but context rot is real: performance degrades significantly as input token count increases regardless of which model is used. The goal of context engineering is to give the agent exactly the right information, in the right structure, at the right time so it can reliably complete high-value tasks with minimal errors and supervision.

segments.heading: Context poisoning, the Goldilocks zone, and compounding errors
segments.text: Bad context compounds in long-horizon tasks. A single agent with 95% accuracy drops to approximately 86% across three sequential decisions (0.95^3). Context too sparse: the agent hallucinates, asks excessive clarifying questions, and reasons from outdated facts. Context too dense: slower responses, higher API costs, distraction, and noise. Context poisoning is the extreme case where malicious or incorrect instructions embedded in context override the agent's intended behavior. The Goldilocks zone is the right amount of context, properly structured, for the current task.

segments.heading: Three strategies to dynamically manage the context window: tools, skills, session compaction
segments.text: Tools are executable functions the agent calls to retrieve external context. Tool schema definitions (when to call, what parameters) add tokens to the context window, so tool-heavy agents embed most of their intelligence in tool definitions. Skills (ADK concept) use progressive disclosure: only a skill title and description (Level 1 metadata) are loaded initially. When the agent invokes a skill, the full skill instructions are loaded. This is more token-efficient than including all tools upfront. Session compaction removes stale prior turns from context as the conversation grows, using LLM-driven summarization to extract meaningful content from verbose turn logs without losing important information.

segments.heading: ADK working context: how the context window is assembled
segments.text: ADK has the concept of a working context: an ephemeral, just-in-time compilation that is thrown out after every model invocation. It assembles from: (1) conversation history from session storage (Vertex AI Session Service) with compaction applied; (2) developer-provided system instructions, tool definitions, and skill definitions; (3) memories retrieved from Memory Bank, injected either into the session history (via tool calls) or into system instructions for always-on context.

segments.heading: Memory Bank: agentic long-term memory as a managed service
segments.text: Memory Bank is a managed Vertex AI Agent Platform service for long-term, cross-session memory. The workflow: the agent streams events to Memory Bank during conversation. Memory Bank decouples ingestion from processing so the agent is not slowed by memory extraction. A memory extraction LLM processes the conversation, extracts meaningful facts, and consolidates new memories with existing ones for the same user (by user ID scope). Consolidation prevents duplicate memories and maintains a single source of truth. Memory generation rules (for example, extract after 10 minutes of inactivity) are configurable. Memory scopes can be user-level, session-level, or department-level.

segments.heading: Memory profiles: structured schemas for precomputed context
segments.text: Memory profiles are a new Memory Bank feature providing structured memory with a developer-defined Pydantic schema. Instead of unstructured natural language snippets, profiles define fields (for example, preferred communication style, travel preferences) and Memory Bank extracts and populates those fields from conversation history. Benefits: predictable schema means system instructions can reference known fields directly; rollback to previous profile versions is supported; individual memory entries can be inspected to see how they evolved from source conversations. Two memory injection patterns: just-in-time retrieval via a tool call when the agent decides it is needed, and always-on context loading the profile into system instructions at session start.

segments.heading: AT&T case study: multi-channel, multi-session customer sales agent
segments.text: AT&T's product catalog is highly complex (hundreds of phone models, multiple wireless plan tiers, fiber plans, bundled products). Human sales agents have short tenures (under a year) and cannot hold the full catalog in memory. Customers make purchase decisions across multiple sessions and multiple channels (web, chat, IVR, retail, call center). The AI agent architecture uses an orchestrator that identifies customer intent and routes to expert subagents (defined by skill, not product line). The logical layer is separated from the display layer (formatter adapts output per channel). Context is tightly curated per agent with thinking budget controls. DLP encrypts PII before it reaches the LLM and decrypts on the way back. Memory Bank and Vertex AI Session Service provide short and long-term memory across sessions and channels. A customer browsing on day 1 and returning on day 3 via a different channel receives recommendations that continue from where the previous session left off. The agent is hyper-personalized at individual line level (not account level). The production app is live in the AT&T flagship mobile app for device upgrades.

title: Build an AI Agent knowledge base using SQL (BigQuery + Gemini)
description: Episode 1 of a multi-part Hands On AI series demonstrating how to build an AI agent knowledge base directly using BigQuery and Gemini. Walks through creating BigQuery external tables to query raw text files in Cloud Storage without copying data, using ML.GENERATE_TEXT to prompt Gemini inside SQL, and parsing nested JSON responses into normalized relational tables.

segments.heading: Hands-on project overview: unstructured to structured ELT pipeline
segments.text: The lab demonstrates how to convert unstructured text files stored in Google Cloud Storage into structured, queryable tables in BigQuery using Gemini models called directly from SQL. In this two-part series, the resulting structured bestiary dataset is prepared as an analytical knowledge base for downstream RAG agents running on Cloud Run.

segments.heading: Environment setup and BigQuery external tables
segments.text: Setting up the project involves activating Cloud Shell, enabling core APIs (BigQuery, Cloud Storage, AI Platform, Dataflow), and establishing a BigQuery Connection service account. Using BigQuery external tables allows querying raw CSV and text files residing in Cloud Storage as virtual tables without duplicating data across environments. External tables dynamically reflect new files added to the storage bucket while preserving central governance.

segments.heading: Invoking Gemini via BQML ML.GENERATE_TEXT
segments.text: A remote model reference pointing to Gemini 2.5 Flash is created in BigQuery via the remote connection. The ML.GENERATE_TEXT SQL function executes prompt instructions across every row of the external table in parallel. The prompt instructs Gemini to extract entities (monsters, battles, adventurers) into a strictly formatted JSON object.

segments.heading: JSON parsing, cleansing, and table normalization
segments.text: ML.GENERATE_TEXT outputs candidate text alongside evaluation metadata like token counts and log probabilities. Using BigQuery's built-in PARSE_JSON function and JSON path expressions (for example, JSON_VALUE), the raw output is cleaned and split into distinct normalized tables (monsters, battles, adventurers) ready for SQL analytics and agent retrieval.

title: Navigate the agentic shift in software development with Google
description: Google is Customer Zero for its own developer AI products. In this Cloud Next session, two VPs share what they have actually learned deploying AI coding agents internally at Google with over 100,000 engineers. Covers the 75% AI code stat, real failures and pivots in AI code review strategy, spec-driven development, agent observability and trajectory tracking, and how Google scales AI adoption through AI champions and team-level agents.

segments.heading: Scale of AI-written code at Google
segments.text: Sundar Pichai announced at Cloud Next 2026 that approximately 75% of all new code at Google is written by AI. In the last 12 months, Google added more code than it had in the preceding three years combined. About one-third of all code changes submitted at Google are entirely or almost entirely authored by coding agents (human contribution approximately 1-2% of those changes). GitHub reported a 30% increase in merged pull requests across their corpus over the same period. The enterprise paradox: how do you convert 10x code volume into 10x business value without 10x risk? Code volume growth is putting pressure on code review, testing, and other systems designed for human-scale throughput.

segments.heading: Lessons from building AI code review at Google: three strategies, two failures
segments.text: Approximately 10% of developer time at Google goes into code review. As code volume grew, that percentage held constant, raising concerns about rubber-stamping. First attempt: one central AI review agent catching all issues for all teams. Result: spectacular failure. Models in 2023-2024 were not reliable enough to catch serious issues consistently, and developers pushed back on AI interfering during flow time. Second attempt: specialized agents targeting narrow, well-defined issues (for example, a Python readability agent enforcing Google's style guide). Evals looked great. Result: developer productivity for the Python cohort dropped 9% in the first week of the experiment, because developers found the volume of comments overwhelming. Both extreme approaches failed.

segments.heading: The tiered approach that works: central plus specialized plus shepherding
segments.text: Google's current three-anchor AI review strategy: (1) A central review agent covering a small, universal set of issues applicable to all teams (security, reliability, performance, maintainability). This set is intentionally small. The agent is tunable at individual and team levels for additional specialization. (2) A shepherding agent that monitors in-flight code changes and drives them through the CI/CD pipeline. If a build breaks, the shepherding agent attempts to fix the root cause and re-activates the review agent. It iterates until CI/CD is clear. (3) A risk assessor agent that scans all in-flight changes for risk. High-risk changes are tagged and require mandatory human review. Governance mechanisms for low-risk changes to flow through auto-approvals without human review are also in progress.

segments.heading: Spec-driven development and testing
segments.text: The AI doom loop: approximately 12% of developer time goes to babysitting AI coding agents. Natural language prompts are inherently imprecise, leading to incomplete design, excessive clarifying back-and-forth, and developers letting agents do whatever they want and refactoring later. Spec-driven development addresses this by requiring developers to work with agents upfront to produce a precise requirements specification before code is written. The spec captures design intent, API contracts, constraints, and success criteria. Developers using spec-driven development produce less rework, more exhaustive system designs, and more readable and maintainable code. Spec-driven testing: a testing agent reads existing code and tests, produces a specification document showing current API contracts and pre/post-conditions, highlights missing test coverage, accepts developer feedback on the spec, and then implements the missing tests by editing the test file. The spec is updated to reflect new coverage status.

segments.heading: Agent observability: trajectories, path clustering, and token heat maps
segments.text: Traditional observability is like train tracks: fixed, observable, predictable. Agent observability is like a self-driving car: each run takes a different path. Two altitudes of agent trajectory tracking at Google: (1) Individual trajectory: user inputs across all turns, how the agent interprets inputs, chain-of-thought reasoning, steps taken for each task, and annotated output signals. (2) Aggregate trajectory: path clustering to identify common failure patterns, tool reliability analysis, token heat maps to find inefficiencies and recurring dead ends, tool-set rationalization. Key finding from aggregate trajectory analysis: teams often expose far too many MCP tools initially. Honing in on the critical tool set for specific workflows improved agent reliability and reduced token waste. Benefits observed: developers can redirect stuck agents faster (avoiding the doom loop), system health monitoring, and rapid identification of hotspots.

segments.heading: Scaling AI adoption at Google: AI champions, dashboards, and two agent categories
segments.text: Scaling AI adoption across 100,000 developers with diverse roles (ML, frontend, hardware, distributed systems) requires managing the pace of change. Developers need to shift mental models from syntax to systems. Google's AI Champions program: a network of engaged early adopters who receive knowledge packs, hands-on coaching, and early product access. They share quality signals back to product teams before broad rollout, and spread best practices within their organizations. The program creates two flywheels: a rapid product feedback loop (usage data flows back to Google DeepMind) and a knowledge-spreading flywheel (effective approaches discovered by YouTube teams reach Maps teams). Token use dashboards and adoption rate metrics help teams understand whether AI is being used effectively. Two emerging agent categories: (1) Personal agents running with developer permissions on their computer (Antigravity IDE, Gemini CLI, Cloud Code). (2) Team agents that carry tribal knowledge: team best practices, coding standards, deployment procedures. Both categories require governance, sandboxing, and accountability attribution.

title: Agent development and AgentOps with BigQuery, ADK, and MCP
description: Join this session to learn about Agent Development Kit (ADK) and Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration methods that standardize how agents connect to your data while removing the need to build custom database connectors from scratch. Discover how to build agents with the ADK that access BigQuery for analysis, Google Maps for geospatial insights, and AlloyDB for transactions, all in a single workflow. Learn how to implement agent operations (AgentOps) for deep observability into both agent performance and cost with a single line of code.

segments.heading: Agentic Data Cloud stack: from open-source to managed data agents
segments.text: BigQuery positions its agent connectivity offerings on a stack. At the bottom, raw APIs give full flexibility but require the developer to own value creation. Moving up: (1) Agent Development Kit (ADK) with first-party BigQuery tools, (2) open-source MCP Toolbox, (3) managed remote MCP servers (zero-ops), and (4) first-party data agents with built-in agentic harness. Higher on the stack means more built-in value; lower means more flexibility.

segments.heading: ADK with BigQuery tools: a data agent in under 10 lines
segments.text: A pip install of the ADK package now includes BigQuery function tools in three categories: foundational tools (find tables, get schema, query in multiple modes), advanced tools (forecasting, contribution analysis), and the ability to use an existing data agent as a tool. BigQuery skills are also available in ADK for higher accuracy in data workflows. A working data agent can be built in under 10 lines of Python using block write mode (read-only) and application default credentials.

segments.heading: MCP Toolbox: open-source server with parameterized SQL tools
segments.text: MCP Toolbox is an open-source MCP server with pre-built connectors to multiple data sources including BigQuery. It is configured via YAML and runs locally or remotely. The standout feature is creating custom tools using parameterized SQL: the agent passes parameters instead of generating SQL, making agentic actions more deterministic. Example: a hotel-booking chatbot tool that accepts a hotel name as a parameter rather than allowing the agent to write arbitrary SQL. MCP Toolbox and its tools are available in a stable release.

segments.heading: Managed BigQuery MCP server: zero-ops with IAM governance
segments.text: Google's managed MCP server for BigQuery is available at bigquery.googleapis.com/mcp. It provides two tool sets: read-only tools (blocks all DML and DDL to prevent accidental modifications) and read-write tools (full SQL surface via Execute SQL). Data administrators can apply IAM deny policies to block all read-write tools regardless of what the agent developer configures, keeping data ownership with the platform team. The server integrates with IAM, audit logs, and VPC Service Controls (VPCSC). BigQuery MCP is generally available and used by Anthropic internally and by partners including Glean.

segments.heading: Agent Analytics: one-line observability piped into BigQuery
segments.text: Agent Analytics is an open-source ADK plugin (and a Langgraph callback handler) that streams all agent events to a BigQuery table with a single line of code change. Data includes tool use, latency per step, input and output tokens, and can include multimodal data (images, video, audio) through BigQuery object references. Once in BigQuery, standard SQL gives performance and error views; AI functions in BigQuery enable LLM-as-a-judge evaluations and conversation categorization at scale. A data agent can then be built on top of the agent logs table so teams can query their production agent behavior using natural language.

segments.heading: Demo: bakery-location business consultant agent (BigQuery + Google Maps)
segments.text: Jiaxun Wu demonstrated a business consultant agent for opening a bakery in Los Angeles. The agent uses two managed MCP tools: BigQuery (for traffic data and sales history) and Google Maps (for real-time competitor locations). The agent routes each question to the right tool automatically. Steps: (1) find the zip code with the highest morning traffic using BigQuery, (2) list competing bakeries in that zip code using Google Maps, (3) get top-three best-selling bakery items from sales history using BigQuery. Agent Analytics logged all events in real time. A BigQuery conversational analytics agent then analyzed agent latency and identified that Google Maps place searches were slower than BigQuery queries.

segments.heading: Carrefour case study: data platform support agent with ADK and OAuth
segments.text: Guillaume Blaquiere (Carrefour) built a support agent for the Carrefour data platform (code-named Phenix Darwin) that handles 600-plus internal data consumers via Google Chat. The problem: repetitive questions from new team members draining platform team time. The agent ingests documentation and chat history via Vertex AI Search, manages sessions via Vertex AI Agent Engine (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform), and runs on Cloud Run. BigQuery Agent Analytics provides dashboards on session counts (approximately 200 per week), error rates, latency, and most-used tools. An OAuth flow restricted to direct messages prevents credential sharing in group spaces. Switching from custom Python code to ADK BigQuery toolsets eliminated hundreds of lines of bespoke database introspection code.

segments.heading: Production takeaways: use case selection, proximity, and integration cost
segments.text: Guillaume's three closing lessons: (1) choose the right use case: do not apply AI to every workflow; pick cases where AI delivers clear value. (2) Bring agents to where users already are: integrating the agent into Google Chat rather than a new tool drove immediate adoption. (3) Never underestimate integration cost: connecting agents to legacy applications, especially mainframe systems without APIs, is harder than it appears.

title: AgentOps: Operationalize AI Agents
description: A comprehensive masterclass on operationalizing generative AI agents (AgentOps). Builds upon the evolution from DevOps to MLOps and GenAIOps to establish foundational AgentOps practices: standardized repository structures, multi-environment architectures (Dev, Staging, Prod, Governance), prompt and tool catalogs, Model Armor guardrails, evaluation loops, and tool registry patterns.

segments.heading: Evolution from DevOps and MLOps to GenAIOps and AgentOps
segments.text: DevOps established repository, CI/CD, and automated testing standards for deterministic software. MLOps extended DevOps to non-deterministic model training and deployment. GenAIOps emerged as an umbrella discipline covering Foundation Model Operations (producers) and AI application lifecycle management (consumers). Under GenAIOps, AgentOps specifically tackles multi-step reasoning, tool execution, memory persistence, and dynamic planning.

segments.heading: Multi-environment enterprise architecture for AI systems
segments.text: Robust AI operations require four distinct environment layers: (1) Infrastructure and networking (VPCs, IAM, Terraform); (2) Data Lake / Data Mesh (ETL pipelines, RAG stores, prompt catalogs); (3) Compute environments (Sandbox for research, Development for building, Staging for integration testing, Production for user traffic); (4) Governance (central Model Registry, code repositories, artifact stores, audit dashboards).

segments.heading: GenAIOps workflows: prompt catalog, model selection, and guardrails
segments.text: Enterprises filter thousands of public models down to approved sets evaluated on custom datasets across precision, latency, and cost (such as choosing Gemini Flash over Pro for speed and cost efficiency). A Prompt Catalog versions prompts and test cases. The backend application implements caching, auto context retrieval (RAG), telemetry monitoring, and safety guardrails (using Model Armor to prevent prompt injection and redact PII).

segments.heading: Agent core mechanics: function calling and runtime loops
segments.text: An agent core consists of a foundation model, system instructions, and declared tool schemas. When given a query, the model outputs structured function call parameters. The agent runtime executes the function against underlying APIs or code, feeds the tool output back to the model, and iterates until the final response is constructed.

segments.heading: AgentOps evaluation, tool registries, and repository standardization
segments.text: Agent evaluation tests tool selection accuracy, parameter extraction validity, answer grounding, and operational latency. Tool Registries (using Apigee API Hub and Firestore) centralize and govern code tools, data tools, and API tools with unified authentication. Standardized repository layouts organize modular tools, agent prompts, eval scripts, and deployment configurations into reproducible CI/CD pipelines.

title: AI agents for data engineering and data science | The Agent Factory Podcast
description: Episode of The Agent Factory Podcast covering new agent developments. Discusses the Gemini Computer Use model for browser automation and CodeMender for autonomous code vulnerability remediation. Demos the BigQuery Data Engineering Agent (Dataform declarative pipelines, time dimensions, quality assertions), the Data Science Agent in Colab Enterprise (isolation forest anomaly detection), and an ADK app using Spanner graph traversal and Nano Banana image generation.

segments.heading: Industry update: Gemini Computer Use model and CodeMender
segments.text: The Gemini API introduced a computer use model capable of taking screen captures and returning UI actions (click, type, scroll, navigate) with integrated safety confirmations for sensitive steps. CodeMender is an autonomous security agent operating in reactive mode (patching active zero-days found by tools like Big Sleep and OSS-Fuzz) and proactive mode (refactoring entire vulnerability classes), having upstreamed 72 verified security patches to open-source codebases.

segments.heading: Data Science Agent in Colab Enterprise: anomaly detection
segments.text: The Data Science Agent in Colab Enterprise takes natural language prompts and generates end-to-end exploratory data science workflows. In the demo, the agent loads BigQuery tables, structures pre-processing pipelines, trains an Isolation Forest model to detect statistical anomalies in customer support cases, and generates charts with actionable explanations.

segments.heading: BigQuery Data Engineering Agent: Dataform pipelines and quality assertions
segments.text: The BigQuery Data Engineering Agent operates on Dataform declarative pipeline files stored in Git repositories. The agent generates SQL definitions calling AI functions (AI.GENERATE with Gemini 2.5 Flash), models time dimensions for natural-language-to-SQL query optimization, and creates automated data quality assertions (such as non-null ID checks and unique constraints) across staging and production tables.

segments.heading: Demo: ADK multi-agent app with Spanner Graph and comic generation
segments.text: An ADK application demonstrates connecting to a Cloud Spanner knowledge graph using GQL and Spanner QA chains. The agent queries Spanner documentation concepts (e.g., regional vs. multi-region configurations), constructs structured comic strip panel scripts, and passes prompts to Nano Banana with an automated multi-step quality checker loop evaluating generated images.

title: AI Agent Infrastructure Decoded
description: Deep dive into the underlying compute and architecture required to build, deploy, and scale enterprise AI agents. Covers test-time thinking compute, matching workloads to CPUs, TPUs, and NVIDIA RTX/GeForce GPUs, and four Google Cloud deployment paths (Cloud Run, GKE Agent Sandbox, Agent Runtime, and GKE). Concludes with a live multi-agent drug discovery demo (Bio-Forge) using NVIDIA Nemotron and DiffDock on GKE.

segments.heading: What defines an AI agent and why enterprise adoption converged
segments.text: Unlike simple chatbots that return static text responses to prompts, agents take high-level goals, formulate plans, execute tools, observe environment feedback, and loop until completion. Enterprise agent maturity converged due to three factors: (1) advanced reasoning models capable of multi-step tool calling, (2) open standardized protocols (MCP for tools/data and A2A for inter-agent communication), and (3) mature platform orchestration and governance runtimes (ADK and Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform).

segments.heading: Inference evolution: thinking compute and matching hardware to agent tasks
segments.text: The AI frontier has shifted from training larger models to allocating compute at inference (test-time compute or thinking budgets). Models like Gemini 3 generate scripts, execute in sandboxes, read error logs, and iterate before returning verified answers. Compute requirements split across components: orchestration and glue logic run efficiently on commodity CPUs; text reasoning calls managed TPU-backed APIs; complex simulations and molecular rendering require high-throughput GPUs (NVIDIA RTX 6000 Pro with confidential computing).

segments.heading: Four Google Cloud deployment patterns for AI agents
segments.text: Architectures sit across a spectrum from serverless simplicity to full infrastructure control: (1) Cloud Run: serverless speed, scales to zero, ideal for spiky traffic, ADK APIs, and A2A endpoints; (2) GKE Agent Sandbox: gVisor kernel-isolated execution for safely running untrusted agent-generated code at scale; (3) Agent Runtime: managed enterprise runtime providing out-of-the-box session management, Memory Bank, tracing, and IAM; (4) Raw GKE: maximum customization for specialized GPU clusters and custom containerized inference microservices (NIMs).

segments.heading: Enterprise security ground-up and decision framework
segments.text: Security requires multi-layer defense: Confidential GPUs at the silicon layer, VPC Service Controls at the network perimeter, SPIFFE-based Agent Identity, Model Armor edge content filtering against prompt injections, and Cloud audit logs. Decision tree: use RAG when closing a knowledge gap, fine-tuning (SFT/LoRA) for behavioral or formatting gaps, Model-as-a-Service for general capabilities, and self-hosted GPU endpoints for strict residency or high-volume unit economics.

segments.heading: Demo: Bio-Forge multi-agent drug discovery on GKE and Gemini Enterprise
segments.text: A multi-agent biomedical system (Bio-Forge) demonstrates accelerating leukemia drug discovery: (1) An orchestrator agent queries the UniProt database via specialized tools to fetch human ABL1 kinase sequences; (2) A lead agent calls an NVIDIA DiffDock microservice running on GKE GPU nodes to perform 3D molecular docking simulations of Imatinib; (3) Agent-to-UI renders interactive 3D protein binding poses; (4) Lead optimization models generate 8 new drug variants; (5) Gemini performs safety synthesis to evaluate cardiotoxicity and recommend against unviable candidates before in-vitro trials.

title: How to build AI agents with memory
description: Join Google's Sita Lakshmi Sangameswaran and Kimberly Milam, the tech lead for Vertex AI Memory Bank, as they walk you through the complete playbook for building agents that remember. You will learn the difference between volatile and persistent memory, how to generate, store, and retrieve information across conversations, and even how to customize your agent's memory with a time-to-live (TTL).

segments.heading: The problem of forgetful agents: volatile vs. persistent memory
segments.text: Sita Lakshmi Sangameswaran and Kimberly Milam (Tech Lead for Vertex AI Memory Bank) discuss why stateless AI agents are expensive and frustrating for users. Repeatedly explaining context inflates token budgets across sessions. While volatile in-memory storage maintains turn-by-turn context strictly within an active session, production architectures require persistent memory services to extract, consolidate, and retrieve semantic facts across multi-session user lifecycles.

segments.heading: ADK memory architecture: BaseMemoryService, InMemory, and Memory Bank
segments.text: The Agent Development Kit (ADK) standardizes memory via BaseMemoryService, exposing two primary methods: add_session_to_memory (extracting and storing session facts) and search_memory (querying stored facts via similarity search). While the development-oriented InMemoryMemoryService simply dumps raw conversation dictionaries into local memory without filtering, Vertex AI Memory Bank acts as an asynchronous, managed service that runs background extraction LLM chains (e.g., using Gemini 2.5 Flash) to distill raw turns into high-signal atomic facts.

segments.heading: Memory lifecycle: background extraction and automatic consolidation
segments.text:
Vertex AI Memory Bank operates in the background through two automated stages:

1. Extraction: An LLM analyzes session turns, discarding irrelevant chitchat while extracting meaningful facts, preferences, and task outcomes.
2. Consolidation: The service compares extracted facts against existing user memories. It deduplicates redundant data, merges complementary updates (e.g., updating a generic bike preference to a red balance bike), and resolves contradictions without bloating the vector corpus.

segments.heading: Retrieval patterns: Preload Memory Tool vs. Load Memory Tool vs. Callbacks
segments.text:
Developers have three distinct options for injecting persistent memories into agent context:

- Preload Memory Tool: Runs deterministically before agent execution, injecting relevant user memories directly into the system prompt.
- Load Memory Tool: Exposed as an on-demand function call; the LLM explicitly chooses whether to query memory when incoming queries require historical context.
- Custom Callbacks: Developers define granular pre-invocation hooks using the Agent Engine SDK to execute custom similarity searches across specific scope keys (app_name and user_id).

segments.heading: Custom memory extraction: managed topics vs. custom business topics
segments.text: By default, Memory Bank filters facts into four managed topics: personal information, user preferences, key conversation events/task outcomes, and explicit instructions to remember/forget. Developers can customize extraction by creating domain-specific custom topics with descriptive labels and few-shot examples (e.g., capturing structured customer feedback on coffee shop offerings while ignoring general conversational dialogue).

segments.heading: Memory governance: Time-to-Live (TTL) and lifecycle management
segments.text: To comply with data privacy policies and prevent stale context buildup, Memory Bank supports Time-to-Live (TTL) policies. Developers can configure global default TTLs (e.g., 30 days) across an entire Agent Engine instance or define granular operational TTLs that establish expiration timers only upon memory creation without resetting timers during subsequent consolidation updates.

title: The intersection of AI, art, and design with Douglas Edric Stanley and Anthony Masure
description: Join Ashley Oldacre as she hosts a conversation with artist Douglas Edric Stanley and Dean of Research at Geneva University of Art and Design Anthony Masure. They discuss their origin stories, the role of AI in creative fields, and the value of critical thinking in a technology-driven world.
entities: Geneva University of Art and Design (HEAD Geneve)

segments.heading: Origins across Silicon Valley hacker culture, French philosophy, and media labs
segments.text: Douglas Edric Stanley (new media artist and professor) and Anthony Masure (Dean of Research at Geneva University of Art and Design, HEAD Geneve) recount their career paths. Growing up in 1970s Silicon Valley with mainframe teletype machines and early Atari prototypes, Stanley transitioned to Paris to study post-structuralist philosophy before curating early digital art at the Centre Pompidou and developing creative coding curricula. Masure established research on the politics of design, blockchain, and artificial intelligence.

segments.heading: Cybernetic loops and the temporality of human-machine interaction
segments.text: Stanley examines how technological artifacts shape human perceptions of time. Unlike novels or cinema which have predefined linear conclusions, digital systems operate on continuous cybernetic clock cycles where states recurse infinitely (such as save-and-retry gameplay loops in video games). Interacting with algorithmic systems creates recursive feedback loops where human cognitive models shape code, and algorithmic outputs subsequently reshape cultural thought patterns.

segments.heading: The role of the designer: holistic context vs. automated optimization
segments.text: The panel explores the fundamental difference between design methodology and automated AI generation. True design requires interpreting client briefs within unique cultural, generational, and institutional contexts rather than retrieving generic statistical averages from past datasets. While generative tools output polished artifacts instantly, design education emphasizes understanding underlying problem spaces, materials, and human relational dynamics.

segments.heading: Resisting late-capitalist maintenance: preserving the craft of drawing
segments.text: Stanley cautions against over-optimizing creative workflows into button-pushing interfaces where humans become mere maintainers of generative machines. In a collaborative project with Swiss art utensil manufacturer Caran d'Ache, researchers investigated how AI can be injected subtly into physical sketching without interrupting the somatic pleasure and cognitive flow of drawing on paper.

segments.heading: Hybrid strategies: AI as an experimental medium rather than a turnkey tool
segments.text: Discussing the exhibition Assembling Intelligence - Hybrid Strategies for AI, Art, and Design, Stanley details diverse student approaches: retraining local language models to deliver generative 3D sculpting prompts, exploring prompt-output discordances as poetic commentary, and combining machine learning predictions with traditional physical ceramics and oil paintings. The panel argues that AI serves best as an idiosyncratic creative medium rather than a standardized productivity substitute.

segments.heading: Ancient roots of generative text: from the I Ching to non-linear narratives
segments.text: Stanley contextualizes modern large language models within millennia of human fascination with non-human generative oracles. Ancient systems like the I Ching used physical randomization (yarrow sticks) to assemble textual divination, reflecting human tendencies toward pareidolia and longing for dialogue with external intelligences. Modern generative models unlock real-time non-linear interactive storytelling where dynamic narratives synthesize adaptively around reader agency.

title: How to use AI for your job search | Google Career Certificates
description: Comprehensive practical guide from Google Career Certificates on using generative AI tools across the entire job search lifecycle. Covers identifying transferable skills, building career identity statements with Career Dreamer, structuring actionable job search plans with Gemini, writing tailored and measurable resumes, managing professional online presence, and preparing for behavioral interviews.

segments.heading: Introduction: structuring the modern job search with AI
segments.text: The average US job search takes around 20 weeks and involves hundreds of application rounds. Generative AI tools (Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude) act as collaborative assistants to simplify and organize the process: identifying transferable skills, drafting career identity statements, building search plans, tailoring resumes, and practicing interview scenarios.

segments.heading: Identifying transferable skills and skills-based hiring
segments.text: Employers increasingly adopt skills-based hiring practices, prioritizing verified competencies over rigid degree credentials. Transferable skills (communication, problem solving, teamwork, data analysis) are uncovered through a three-step reflection: examining life and work experiences, isolating specific capabilities built during those roles, and mapping those capabilities to target job requirements.

segments.heading: Career identity statements and the Career Dreamer tool
segments.text: A career identity statement acts as a North Star, summarizing a candidate's skills, background, and professional goals in a concise, authentic paragraph for bios, elevator pitches, and cover letters. Career Dreamer (grow.google/careerdreamer) uses Lightcast labor market data and generative AI to extract transferable skills from prior jobs, generate tailored identity statements, and suggest aligned career pathways.

segments.heading: Building a customized job search plan with Gemini
segments.text: Job seekers with structured search plans are 30% more likely to receive offers. Prompting Gemini with a target role, available weekly hours, and a career identity statement produces an iterative step-by-step roadmap covering company research, portfolio updates, application targets, and follow-up cadence.

segments.heading: Resume best practices: content, structure, and AI tailoring
segments.text: Recruiters spend an average of 7.4 seconds reviewing a resume. Key principles: (1) Content: lead with measurable business impact (quantifiable metrics), strong action verbs, and clear context; (2) Structure: concise 1-2 page layout, scannable bullet points, and prominent skill keywords matching the target job description; (3) Personalization: iteratively tailoring resume bullets to specific job postings rather than submitting generic applications.

segments.heading: Building and curating a professional online presence
segments.text: An online presence acts as an always-on personal brand. Candidates should actively engage in industry discussions, publish project portfolios (GitHub for developers, Behance for designers, LinkedIn for general networking), audit personal privacy settings, and use AI prompts to identify relevant industry platforms and communities.

title: Power intelligent agents with AI-native databases
description: Explores how AI-native databases transform enterprise data into active agent context. Covers the convergence of operational databases and warehouses, multimodal search, graph RAG, and natural language interfaces. Features a fireside chat with Anthropic's David Soria Parra on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and showcases Google Cloud pre-built data agents.

segments.heading: The inflection point: AI-native databases vs. legacy data silos
segments.text: For the first time in the 50-year history of databases, AI is fundamentally redefining what data systems do. Legacy architectures trap enterprise knowledge in disconnected operational databases and analytical warehouses, making it difficult for agents to query cross-silo context. AI-native databases break down these boundaries by unifying operational storage, vector indexes, knowledge graphs, and model execution directly within the database engine.

segments.heading: Superpowers of AI-native databases: search, graph RAG, and multimodal context
segments.text: AI-native databases provide high-fidelity context through four capabilities: (1) Hybrid search combining lexical BM25 with dense semantic vector retrieval, (2) Natural language querying that translates intent into safe SQL/GQL, (3) Multimodal search indexing images, video, and audio alongside relational tables, and (4) Graph RAG uncovering complex relationship paths across entity networks.

segments.heading: Fireside chat with David Soria Parra on Model Context Protocol (MCP)
segments.text: Anthropic's David Soria Parra discusses the origins and rapid adoption of MCP. Rather than requiring developers to write custom point-to-point API connectors for every model and tool, MCP standardizes how language models discover data schemas, execute tool queries, and receive structured context securely across enterprise boundaries.

segments.heading: Google Cloud pre-built data agents and enterprise adoption
segments.text: Google Cloud provides pre-built data agents that integrate out of the box with BigQuery and operational stores. These agents automate database optimization, monitor data quality, assist with complex query formulation, and safely expose business intelligence to non-technical users via governed Agent Platform interfaces.

title: Power intelligent agents with AI-native databases
description: AI-native databases are essential for powering agents with enterprise data. Learn how they enable highly relevant context, automate operations, and manage risk. In this session, we examine AI-powered search, natural language interfaces, multimodal queries, and graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG). These move beyond simple retrieval, providing agents with high-fidelity, interconnected context. Discover how open standards like Model Context Protocol (MCP) and agentic IDEs streamline workflows for rapid, reliable deployment of agents.
entities: ScaNN index (Google proprietary approximate nearest neighbor index)

segments.heading: The case for an agentic data cloud: from system of insight to system of action
segments.text: Legacy data architectures are walled gardens of disconnected warehouses and siloed operational databases. Agents require seamless access to data from multiple sources and semantic context that gives meaning to the data. The current paradigm of moving data to AI creates lag and manual integration cost. Google's strategy is the reverse: move AI to data. The result is the Agentic Data Cloud, a vertically integrated data and AI stack with three properties: AI-native (TPUs invoked for inference within database workloads, models embedded in SQL, data agents in the agentic layer), flexible (Postgres compatibility, run anywhere with AlloyDB Omni), and trusted (enterprise semantic knowledge as context, strict privacy and governance guardrails).

segments.heading: AlloyDB as an AI-native database: vector, hybrid, and AI search
segments.text: AlloyDB is 100% PostgreSQL-compatible and adds Google-specific AI primitives. It supports multimodal data types (structured, text, images, video as embeddings, time series, graph models) and multiple access modalities (vector search, full-text search, forecasting, anomaly detection). Key features: (1) ScaNN index: Google's proprietary approximate nearest neighbor index used in Google Search and YouTube, supporting 10 billion-plus vectors and substantially outperforming plain pgvector. (2) Columnar engine integration boosting pgvector by up to 4x without configuration changes. (3) BM25-based hybrid search: combining vector search and full-text search in a single SQL query. (4) AI functions: SQL functions powered by Gemini for tasks like reranking search candidates by relevance to a nuanced query (for example, shirts suitable for summer in Santorini), sentiment analysis, summarization, and forecasting with the TimesFM model.

segments.heading: TimesFM: forecasting as a database SQL function
segments.text: TimesFM is Google's foundational model pre-trained on time series data. Integrated into AlloyDB as a SQL AI function called forecast, it can produce time series forecasts in seconds on queries that previously required minutes or days. Example query: ask for a sales forecast for all red shoes. AlloyDB performs vector search to find product rows semantically similar to red shoes, fetches the time series for those products, and feeds them into TimesFM to produce a projection. This pipeline is invoked from a single SQL query; the database internally routes inference work to TPUs.

segments.heading: target.com case study: 20% search relevance improvement with AlloyDB
segments.text: target.com migrated their entire search traffic to AlloyDB to improve online search relevance. Using the ScaNN index and dynamic SQL filters on complex data types, they reported a 20% improvement in search relevance. The performance for filtered search queries exceeded what was achievable by manually integrating a relational database with a dedicated vector search engine.

segments.heading: Spanner and GraphRAG for relationship-aware retrieval
segments.text: Spanner extends AI-native search into graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG). Graph models capture relationships among entities: for example, a product's category relationships, supply chain links, or user-behavior connections. In AlloyDB and Spanner, the graph model is virtual and layered over the existing SQL model. Developers do not need to copy or migrate data to a separate graph database. Hybrid search (vector plus full-text) coupled with graph traversal provides agents with interconnected, relationship-aware context that plain vector retrieval cannot.

segments.heading: Data Agent Platform: bridging natural language to SQL with near-100% accuracy
segments.text: The Data Agent Platform addresses three gaps in natural language to SQL conversion: the accuracy gap (many applications require near-100% accuracy), the security gap (lack of in-database granular access control forces developers to build custom security layers), and the scaffolding burden. The Query Data tool reaches near-100% accuracy through three context types: schema ontologies (describing the database schema), query blueprints (developer-injected nuanced interpretations for specific question fragments), and value searches (disambiguating questions against actual data values). Google holds the top rank on the BIRD benchmark for natural language to SQL using schema ontologies alone.

segments.heading: Parameterized Secure Views: deterministic security for agent-generated SQL
segments.text: A naive text-to-SQL approach is vulnerable: an attacker can craft a question that causes the agent to generate SQL joining the user's table to other users' data. Parameterized Secure Views are virtual SQL views that expose only the current end user's data by design. The view is parameterized by user identity, so the agent can only query data scoped to the authenticated user. This is a deterministic security guardrail, not a heuristic one, and is efficient because views are virtual and carry no storage overhead.

segments.heading: MCP strategy: managed servers, MCP Toolbox, and protocol steering
segments.text: Google's MCP approach has three tracks. First, fully managed MCP servers for virtually every Data Cloud service (AlloyDB, Cloud SQL, Spanner, BigQuery, Cloud Storage, analytics services): zero-ops, with IAM, audit logging, Model Armor data protection, and governance controls built in. Second, open-source MCP Toolbox for Databases: stable 1.0 release, 14,000 GitHub stars, 100-plus contributors, 40-plus data sources including Oracle and MongoDB. Third, active participation in MCP steering committees alongside Anthropic to evolve the protocol. Upcoming MCP features include serving agent skills over MCP servers (domain-specific knowledge bundled with the server) and long-running task support.

segments.heading: Fireside chat with David Soria Parra (Anthropic, MCP co-creator)
segments.text: David Soria Parra explains why MCP succeeded: the ecosystem needed a connective layer between frontier models and enterprise data and tools. Companies did not want to build integrations ten times; MCP provided a standard once-and-done integration point. Building MCP servers is intentionally simple to lower adoption friction. On AI-native databases: agents are very good at selecting from large inputs once they have them, but getting to the right first layer of input is difficult. Native database AI primitives (vector search, hybrid search, graph traversal) give agents the toolset to do that retrieval work themselves without developers hand-crafting SQL for each case. Anthropic uses AlloyDB internally and benefits from its enterprise security features combined with the open MCP protocol.

segments.heading: Pre-built data agents from Google: builders, operators, and business users
segments.text: Google offers a suite of pre-built agents covering every data role. For builders: the Data Agent Kit provides agent skills, MCP Toolbox, and IDE extensions; AI Studio now supports Firestore as an underlying database, with Cloud SQL for Postgres support coming. For operators: a Database Observability Agent automates database management by converting complex metrics into actionable insights; Database Center provides real-time fleet visibility; a Database Testing Agent automatically tests performance impact of application and configuration changes. For business users: the Conversational Analytics Agent allows natural language querying of operational AlloyDB and Cloud SQL databases directly from the Cloud Console, with security enforced by Parameterized Secure Views.

title: How AI is revolutionizing sign language recognition with Sam Sepah and Thad Starner
description: Episode of the People of AI podcast featuring Sam Sepah (Google AI/ML Research Manager) and Thad Starner (Georgia Tech Professor and wearable computing pioneer). Explores the 30-year evolution of wearable AI, computer vision for sign language recognition, the impact of language deprivation on deaf children, and educational tools like PopSign AI built to help hearing parents learn American Sign Language.
entities: National Technical Institute for the Deaf (NTID)

segments.heading: Pioneering wearable computing and early augmented reality
segments.text: Thad Starner shares his early journey into AI, from reading Pamela McCorduck's Machines Who Think at age 14 to building custom wearable computers in 1993. His early 'Remembrance Agent' displayed contextually relevant past notes in real-time during conversations, an early predecessor to modern augmented reality demonstrated to Larry Page and Sergey Brin in 1998.

segments.heading: Evolution of Google Glass and accessibility captioning
segments.text: Starner joined Google to lead technical development on Google Glass, evolving bulky 10kg prototypes into lightweight 42g wearable displays. Glass explored real-time speech-to-text captions for deaf and hard-of-hearing users, leading to Starner's collaboration with Google accessibility leader Sam Sepah.

segments.heading: The critical stakes of language acquisition and deaf education
segments.text: Sam Sepah recounts losing his hearing to spinal meningitis at 14 months and his parents' journey learning sign language across Iran, Germany, and the United States. With over 95% of deaf infants born to hearing parents, lack of early visual language access frequently causes Language Deprivation Syndrome, resulting in developmental, cognitive, and employment hurdles. Teaching infant signing (baby sign) accelerates cognitive development in both deaf and hearing children.

segments.heading: Computer vision for ASL: from Hidden Markov Models to PopSign AI
segments.text: Starner's early master's thesis demonstrated the first camera-based phrase-level sign language recognizer using Hidden Markov Models. Modern AI breakthroughs and Google Kaggle competitions enabled PopSign AI, an educational smartphone mobile game that uses real-time computer vision to teach hearing parents foundational ASL vocabulary in their homes.

title: Darren Aronofsky and Demis Hassabis on storytelling in the age of AI
description: Fireside discussion between filmmaker Darren Aronofsky (Primordial Soup) and Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis exploring how generative video models (Veo 3) and world models expand creative storytelling. Covers the philosophy of 'Make soup, not slop,' intentional hallucination, AI as digital collage, and features director Eliza McNitt discussing Ancestra, an emotional hybrid film combining live-action cinematography with AI-generated visuals trained on personal family archives via LoRA.

segments.heading: Make soup, not slop: creative philosophy and partnership
segments.text: Darren Aronofsky and Demis Hassabis announce a partnership between production company Primordial Soup and Google DeepMind. Aronofsky emphasizes that while generative tools produce endless visual novelties, true cinema requires emotional depth and patient storytelling. DeepMind seeks deep collaboration with world-class artists to shape generative video tools (Veo 3) to serve authentic creative expression rather than generic digital noise.

segments.heading: Generative video, world models, and intentional hallucination
segments.text: Demis Hassabis explains that generative video models like Veo represent a crucial stepping stone toward building world models that deeply understand physical dynamics (light, gravity, materials). In informational search, hallucinations are errors; in artistic creation, hallucination equals imagination. Aronofsky and Hassabis discuss adding intentional hallucination controls to encourage creative accidents and exploration.

segments.heading: Creativity beyond Move 37: tool precision vs. human artistry
segments.text: Reflecting on AlphaGo's famous Move 37, Hassabis distinguishes between constrained creative search and true paradigm-shifting human invention (such as formulating General Relativity or inventing the game of Go). Aronofsky compares current generative video workflows to sophisticated digital collage, where human directors curate, prompt, and composite disparate elements into coherent emotional narratives.

segments.heading: Ancestra case study: hybrid filmmaking with Eliza McNitt
segments.text: Director Eliza McNitt presents Ancestra, the first film from the collaboration. The project tells the deeply personal story of her emergency birth, combining live-action performances with Veo generative video. The team used Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning on McNitt's late father's copyrighted 35mm film photography and baby photos to generate emotionally authentic, consenting newborn imagery that would be impossible or unethical to film with real infants.

title: Enable autonomous data agents with BigQuery and Cloud Run
description: A practitioner demo exploring MCP servers for BigQuery, running ADK agents on Cloud Run, and using Gemma 4 as the inference engine for a data agent. Covers the why of MCP (determinism, governance, scalability) versus code generation, Cloud Run execution types (Services, Jobs, Worker Pools, Instances), and a live demo of a Gemma 4-powered agent querying the NYC Citi Bike public dataset to answer complex business questions.

segments.heading: Why MCP and why now: skills vs. tools, determinism, governance
segments.text: The industry has coined many 'X is all you need' claims: agents, MCP, evals, skills. The correct answer is that all of these are needed together. Skills refer to instruction sets that steer agents, but skills still call executable code in the form of tools. The key distinction: when part of a workflow is deterministic, use a deterministic tool rather than non-deterministic code generation. MCP tools are deterministic, explicitly callable, and relatively easy for LLMs to call correctly using schema definitions. Benefits of properly deployed MCP servers: (1) a unified, standardized way to integrate and observe tools; (2) security, IAM, governance built into the platform rather than built per tool by each team; (3) scalability from local STDIO to production managed endpoints.

segments.heading: Cloud Run execution types for autonomous agents
segments.text: Cloud Run provides four execution types. Services: HTTP-based, request-driven, similar to a traditional web app. Jobs: batch compute, runs a task to completion and stops. Worker Pools: long-running processes that wait for messages (Pub/Sub or storage events) and react; no HTTP endpoint exposed. Instances (newly announced at Cloud Next 2026): similar to Jobs but can run for extended durations and spin up very quickly, making them well-suited for autonomous, long-running agent tasks. Cloud Run Sandbox: both open-source sandbox and a new official sandbox for isolated, secure code execution within Cloud Run were announced.

segments.heading: ADK autonomous agent support via Eventarc and Pub/Sub
segments.text: ADK now supports invoking agents via special endpoints on the ADK API server that can be triggered by Pub/Sub messages or Eventarc events. This enables truly autonomous agents: rather than waiting for a synchronous HTTP request, the agent can be triggered by an event (for example, a new file appearing in Cloud Storage, or a scheduled Pub/Sub message) and run a full session without a human present. Combined with Cloud Run Instances or Worker Pools, this creates the foundation for long-running agentic pipelines.

segments.heading: Demo: Gemma 4 data agent querying NYC Citi Bike on BigQuery MCP
segments.text: The demo agent runs on Cloud Run and is powered by a self-hosted Gemma 4 31B instance deployed with the vLLM framework on RTX 6000 Pro GPUs. It has a single tool: the BigQuery MCP server. The dataset is the NYC Citi Bike public dataset (stations and trips tables). First question: 'What data do you have?' The agent calls BigQuery MCP list_tables, gets the schema, and answers. Authentication: the agent does not initially have access to execute BigQuery jobs; an OAuth sign-in flow is triggered from the ADK front end, and after the user authenticates, the agent continues. Second question: 'How can I increase revenue? Suggest up to 10 locations.' The agent reasons about the data, attempts to join stations and trips by station ID, discovers the IDs are of different types (the join fails), self-corrects by joining on station name strings, executes additional SQL to compute usage by subscriber vs. customer type and by station capacity, and produces a ranked list of recommendations. Notable station: Broadway and 36th Street had only 3 docking slots despite approximately 5,000 trips per dock. Gemma 4 showed strong reasoning for a self-hosted open model.

title: Build AI agents at scale with Google Cloud
description: Cloud Next 2026 spotlight session on scaling enterprise AI agents from prototype to global production. Covers the enhanced Agent Runtime (subsecond warm starts, long-running 7-day workflows), Agent Studio, Agent Identity, Agent Gateway, and Memory Bank. Includes a live interactive conference badge-scanning demo by Addy Osmani and enterprise case studies from Shopify (Sidekick agent co-founder) and HCA Healthcare (nurse shift handoff assistant).

segments.heading: The paradigm shift: moving from instructions to goals
segments.text: Brian Delahunty opens with an analogy from his childhood farm: delegation requires defining outcomes and boundaries of trust rather than micromanaging step-by-step procedures. True agents figure out the necessary actions using available tools without explicit procedural programming. Google Cloud announces the unified Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, integrating Vertex AI, ADK, and DeepMind models to scale agentic workloads across Build, Scale, Govern, and Optimize pillars.

segments.heading: Build and Scale: ADK enhancements, Agent Studio, and Agent Runtime GA
segments.text: Developers process over 6 trillion tokens monthly through ADK. New releases include: (1) Graph-based execution engine with dynamic reasoning vs. deterministic controls, (2) native multi-day checkpointing and resumption, (3) Agent Studio low-code visual canvas exporting to ADK code, (4) Agent Runtime GA featuring subsecond cold starts, 7-day long-running execution, and enterprise compliance (CMEK, HIPAA, VPCSC), and (5) persistent Agent Memory Bank mapping custom session IDs to customer records.

segments.heading: Live demo: autonomous swag order agent with runtime tool discovery
segments.text: Addy Osmani builds and deploys an autonomous shopping pipeline live on stage: an Intake Agent analyzes badge photos with Gemini vision, a Stockroom Agent checks BigQuery inventory and triggers automated restock supplier sub-agents, and a Fulfillment Agent dynamically discovers the update_order tool via Agent Registry without hardcoded endpoints. Live conference attendees claim real swag via QR code, showcasing automatic Cloud Run scaling, sub-cent transaction costs, and Model Armor blocking live prompt injection attacks.

segments.heading: Enterprise case studies: Shopify Sidekick and HCA Healthcare nurse handoff
segments.text: Andrew McNamara details Shopify Sidekick, an AI co-founder assisting millions of global merchants using foundational tools, proactive deep research, and an LLM-as-a-judge evaluation rubric passing narrow Turing tests. Sara Liao-Troth presents HCA Healthcare's nurse handoff system across 190 hospitals (80,000 daily handoffs), utilizing a hierarchy of parallel clinical agents, automated citation verifiers, and continuous prompt optimization loops to eliminate communication breakdowns.

title: 3-step approach to mobile app compliance with Checks co-founders Fergus Hurley and Nia Castelly
description: Episode of the People of AI podcast featuring Fergus Hurley and Nia Castelly, co-founders of Checks (Google's AI-powered compliance platform). Discusses the origin of Checks inside Area 120, using NLP and Gemini classifiers to analyze complex privacy policies at scale, and their 3-step compliance framework comparing regulatory mandates, stated developer policies, and live app network telemetry on physical devices.

segments.heading: Founders' backgrounds: from Android Vitals and e-discovery to Area 120
segments.text: Fergus Hurley (entrepreneur, engineer, creator of Android Vitals) and Nia Castelly (Google Play senior product counsel, litigator, computer scientist) share their career journeys. Observing the seismic impact of global regulations like GDPR and CCPA on mobile developers, they recognized that compliance was a major pain point for developers of all sizes, leading them to incubate Checks inside Google's Area 120.

segments.heading: NLP of privacy policies: extracting structured meaning from unstructured legal text
segments.text: Collaborating with NLP privacy researcher Dr. Hamza Harkous, Checks built specialized language models and expert-labeled classifier pipelines. The models extract key data collection and sharing disclosures from long, unstructured privacy policies and terms of service at scale, transforming legal documentation into structured data.

segments.heading: The 3-step Checks compliance triangle
segments.text: Checks automates compliance through a three-prong validation triangle: (1) What the app is legally required to do (GDPR, CCPA, app store policies); (2) What the app says it does (privacy policies and data safety labels extracted via NLP/Gemini); (3) What the app actually does (dynamic network traffic monitoring and static analysis on real physical devices). Any discrepancy between these three vertices triggers actionable alerts in the developer dashboard.

segments.heading: Third-party SDK risks and building trust for digital products
segments.text: Modern mobile apps embed an average of 20 or more third-party SDKs for analytics, ads, and crash reporting. Many compliance violations occur inadvertently when third-party libraries collect permissions or transmit data contrary to the developer's stated policies. Checks inspects live device behavior without requiring code instrumentation, helping developers build consumer trust and meet global privacy standards.

title: Season 5 - Shaping the agentic future with Clement Farabet
description: Join hosts Ashley Oldacre and Christinia Warren as they kick off Season 5 of the People of AI podcast with their first guest, Clement Farabet, VP of Research at Google DeepMind. They discuss the evolution of AI, from early neural networks to the latest advancements in large language models and AI agents. Learn how research and product teams work together to bring developers the best tools to build with and are setting the stage for an agentic future.

segments.heading: From CNN hardware to Twitter and NVIDIA AI infrastructure
segments.text: Clement Farabet (VP of Research at Google DeepMind) recounts his 20-year career across neural network research, custom deep learning hardware, and startups. After completing a PhD under Yann LeCun on real-time computer vision and convolutional architectures, Farabet co-founded Madbits (visual search engine acquired by Twitter in 2014) to build early GPU clusters for large-scale media processing. He subsequently served as VP of AI Infrastructure at NVIDIA, working closely with Jensen Huang on accelerated computing and autonomous driving perception.

segments.heading: The scaling hypothesis and the inevitability of transformers
segments.text: Farabet reflects on architectural shifts in machine learning. Rather than viewing the transformer as an unpredictable anomaly, he considers it an inevitable compute-efficiency optimization on the broader trajectory of the scaling hypothesis. While foundational architectures evolved from CNNs to transformers, the core learning objective remains consistent: exposing neural networks to massive multimodal corpora and scaling training compute by orders of magnitude.

segments.heading: Unifying research and production into a single feedback loop
segments.text: Farabet describes the structural shift in modern AI organizations. Historically, research labs transferred theoretical papers to isolated product teams for downstream re-implementation. Today, frontier AI requires direct integration: Google DeepMind trains unified multimodal foundation checkpoints (Gemini) that directly power production APIs, while real-world application signals from billions of enterprise and consumer interactions feed directly back into model post-training and reinforcement learning.

segments.heading: Defining agency: from passive text generators to virtual interns
segments.text: Farabet defines the transition from passive LLMs to true AI agents around agency: the capacity for models to independently plan, invoke APIs, browse the web, manipulate UIs, and execute multi-step commercial actions. He introduces the operational mental model of treating agents as virtual interns: providing clear goals, establishing bounded sandboxes, and expecting intermediate errors while enabling models to self-critique, reflect, and iterate before committing final outcomes.

segments.heading: Organizational governance, accountability, and agent sandboxing
segments.text: Deploying fleets of thousands of autonomous agents introduces new engineering challenges in organizational governance. Farabet emphasizes that human managers must create structural conditions for agent success without acting as human-in-the-loop bottlenecks for every sub-millisecond execution step. Ensuring safety requires novel computational guardrails, such as append-only operating system abstractions where every agent action produces an immutable audit trace preventing irreversible destructive operations.

segments.heading: Embodied physical robotics vs. unrestricted web agents
segments.text: Farabet contrasts virtual web agents with physical robotics. Paradoxically, embodied robots (where Gemini directly actuates physical arms to grasp objects after few-shot visual demonstrations) are easier to bound and secure because physical kinematics and safety switches impose hard operational constraints. Conversely, unconstrained virtual agents with web and financial access require sophisticated policy enforcement to prevent unintended systemic actions.

segments.heading: Dual model strategy: frontier Gemini APIs and open Gemma weights
segments.text: Farabet details Google DeepMind's complementary release strategy. While frontier capabilities and complex multi-agent orchestration are hosted behind managed Gemini APIs in AI Studio, Google releases open-weights Gemma models to foster open-source academic research and decentralized developer experimentation across local edge environments.

title: Simplified Google Cloud network security: Zero-trust and beyond
description: Comprehensive session on Google Cloud's ML-powered zero-trust network security architecture. Covers Cloud Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW), Cloud Secure Web Proxy with inline Symantec DLP integration, and Cloud Armor edge DDoS protection. Features financial collaboration platform Symphony showcasing their cloud migration security architecture.

segments.heading: The modern threat landscape: securing multi-cloud and distributed applications
segments.text: Over 88% of organizations face major security challenges as workloads distribute across multi-region, multi-cloud, and public-facing environments. A typical enterprise experiences over 60,000 security attacks annually. Cloud network security addresses three primary vectors: protecting distributed application-to-application traffic, securing public-facing global frontends, and protecting hybrid workforces.

segments.heading: Cloud Secure Web Proxy and inline DLP integration
segments.text: Cloud Secure Web Proxy provides a fully managed, serverless egress proxy that enforces granular URL and domain authorization policies for outbound traffic without managing VM fleets or legacy Squid proxies. In partnership with Broadcom, Google Cloud integrates inline Symantec Data Loss Prevention (DLP) directly into Secure Web Proxy and Cloud Load Balancers, inspecting encrypted egress traffic to prevent data exfiltration.

segments.heading: Cloud Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) and intrusion prevention
segments.text: Cloud NGFW embeds advanced threat detection and intrusion prevention services (IPS) natively into the Google Cloud network fabric. It provides distributed, scalable Layer 7 application inspection, automatically blocking known CVE exploits and malicious lateral traffic across VPCs without network re-architecture.

segments.heading: Customer spotlight: Symphony's zero-trust cloud migration
segments.text: Financial communication platform Symphony shares their migration to Google Cloud, detailing how they implemented zero-trust network controls to satisfy strict banking regulatory compliance while maintaining high-throughput, low-latency messaging across hybrid deployments.

title: Build connected AI: Orchestrate tools and agents with registries and ADK
description: Scale is the new challenge for enterprise agent teams: not building agents, but governing hundreds of them. This Cloud Next session covers Agent Registry as the single source of truth for agents and MCP servers, SpecBoost for automatically generating and enriching API specs from logs, Agent Identity with SPIFFE-based per-agent credentials, and a Klook (APAC travel platform) case study showing how they used this stack to build a supply research multi-agent system.

segments.heading: The challenge has shifted: from building agents to governing hundreds
segments.text: Last year at Cloud Next, the challenge was building agents that connect to data sources. A2A was just announced. MCP was new and exciting. The challenge has now shifted: organizations have hundreds of agents that often duplicate work, dozens of MCP servers doing the same thing because teams were each building their own, and no governance layer. Three specific pain points: (1) discoverability: builders cannot find what agents or MCP servers already exist in their organization; (2) building on top: even when they find something, integrating securely is non-trivial; (3) governance: platform teams cannot ensure that only authorized agents call the right set of tools.

segments.heading: Agent Registry: single source of truth for agents, MCPs, and models
segments.text: Agent Registry is the central catalog for all agents, MCP servers, and registered models in a Google Cloud project. It supports registering third-party MCP servers if no existing entry is found. Available via portal UI, API, and SDK. ADK has built-in primitives to discover and call registered agents and MCP servers using just a few lines of code by providing the registry ID. The portal shows: registered agents with their skills and A2A agent card details, registered MCP servers with tool lists and usage metrics, and generated code snippets for ADK integration.

segments.heading: Agent Identity: SPIFFE-based per-agent credentials and secure vault
segments.text: Agent Identity is a SPIFFE-based identity standard that gives each deployed agent its own unique identity (a SPIFFE ID). The identity lifecycle matches the agent lifecycle: created at deployment, revoked when the agent is deleted. This removes the previous pattern where a shared service account was used by all agents in a project, making granular permission management impossible. Agent Identity also includes a Secure Credentials Vault for storing API keys and OAuth credentials per agent, so developers do not need to manage secret sprawl themselves. OAuth configurations (two-legged for service-to-service, three-legged for user-delegated access) are stored in the vault and associated with the specific agent identity.

segments.heading: SpecBoost: from no API specs to enriched, agent-ready MCP servers
segments.text: Enterprise APIs commonly lack rich, accurate OpenAPI specifications. Agents calling underspecified APIs hallucinate parameter names, call endpoints incorrectly, or fail silently. SpecBoost (enabled in API Hub) solves this with three modes: (1) generate: produce API specs from scratch by analyzing API gateway logs (Apigee runtime or Cloud Storage log buckets); (2) boost: take existing specs and enrich them so they are more agent-readable (better descriptions, error examples, parameter semantics); (3) merge: compare generated specs against documentation to detect drift when engineers deploy API changes without updating docs. No spec is published without human sign-off. Vision: API documentation becomes automatically live-updated whenever an API changes. One-click conversion from enriched spec in API Hub to a registered MCP service in Agent Registry is in progress.

segments.heading: Klook case study: supply research multi-agent system
segments.text: Klook is the largest online experiences platform in APAC with 300,000 products across 4,000 destinations and 65 million experiences booked in 2025. The supply research process was manual, slow, and unable to cover the long tail of opportunities. Agents miss seasonal windows (cherry blossom tours, Christmas markets) if insights are delayed by days of manual research. Klook built a multi-agent supply research system: an orchestrator agent coordinates multiple specialized sub-agents, each analyzing a different social platform (one per platform, running in parallel). Key ADK decision: use standalone sub-agents rather than skills for sub-tasks that need their own context and parallel execution. ADK enabled fast wiring. Three learnings: (1) speed: ADK makes new agents fast to build and wire together; (2) reusability: all agents go into Agent Registry so they are discovered by other teams (for example, the YouTube analysis agent also supports voice-of-customer use cases); (3) continuous optimization: non-technical domain experts access published agents via Gemini Enterprise and provide direct feedback. An in-house supply quality agent then evaluates Klook's own catalog against market needs using internal booking data. All internal APIs are being progressively converted to MCP servers and centralized in Agent Registry for governance. Result: workflows that took days now complete in hours.

title: AI tools for human creativity
description: An inside look at Google's latest creative tools from the people using them to make film, art, games, music and more. See how musicians, designers, coders, and filmmakers at Google Creative Lab and Labs are using Google Flow, Antigravity, Genie and Google Flow Music in their creative processes.
entities: Around the World in Good News

segments.heading: Creative Lab's job, and the one thing that is not changing
segments.text:
Matthew Carey and Alex Chen open the first ever builder stage at Google I/O. Both are from Google Creative Lab, a team of writers, designers, coders and filmmakers that collaborates with research and product teams across Google, plays with the latest AI models, and explores the edges of what is possible.

Both came to the work through music. Alex grew up playing viola and piano and making music, and got into coding early, so his whole life has been an attempt to blend code, design and music. Matthew was a choir boy, then a theater kid, then got into making films, then copywriting, then interactive art, which is when he first met Creative Lab.
