segments.heading: Technology as a creative tool through Doug Liman's career
segments.text: Doug Liman frames his relationship with technology as continuous throughout his career. Swingers (1996) was made possible by a new high-speed Kodak film stock that enabled shoestring-budget night-exterior shooting that would not have been feasible two years earlier. He went on to make the first long-form VR series (Invisible, 2015, with Google Cardboard), entering the Guinness Book of World Records for it. He describes his approach as jumping into journeys without knowing how they will end, like guiding whitewater rafting trips where not everyone ends the trip in the boat. He joined Google's AI film initiative 2.5 years ago when Google suggested a short film; he arrived with a full feature script.

segments.heading: Bitcoin: the first fully AI studio feature film
segments.text:
Bitcoin is the first fully AI studio feature film. It stars Casey Affleck as Craig Wright (the man who may or may not have created Bitcoin), Pete Davidson as a billionaire making the biggest financial gamble in history, and Gal Gadot as a reporter trying to determine the truth. The cast includes approximately 125-140 actors across around 150 locations worldwide, significantly more than a typical Bourne Identity-scale film. Liman describes the story's theme as resonant with AI filmmaking: the Bitcoin ethos of trust-verify, do not trust humans but let computers verify, mirrors the tension between human creativity and machine generation in the film's production.

All performances were captured on a single stage over 4.5 weeks of production, following 6 months of prep and R&D. Post-production was initially estimated to take 40 years; it has since been compressed to 6 months, fitting within a conventional film schedule. A 10-minute preview was shown at Cannes before the Google I/O presentation.

segments.heading: How AI removes location and budget constraints for filmmakers
segments.text:
One of the most significant discoveries for Liman was the elimination of the traditional director-producer negotiation over locations and budget. In conventional filmmaking, if a director wants to shoot in Vegas, the producer counters with a basement conference room; trade-offs are constant. With AI-generated environments, Liman realized he could go to Vegas and Antigua in the same film without choosing between them. This changed how he wrote the script: instead of condensing a story to 40 scenes across a manageable number of locations, Bitcoin spans approximately 150 locations because the only constraint is whether each location actually serves the story. He wanted to make Wolf of Wall Street look sleepy in terms of scale and excess.

The expanded location count created more work, not less: 150 locations require characters and people in each one, so casting expanded rather than contracted. Liman explicitly chose not to use any AI-generated performances; every actor in the film is a human being.

segments.heading: The production workflow for Bitcoin
segments.text:
Julina Tatlock served as AI supervisor on set during the capture phase. The workflow:

1. Performances captured on stage with witness cameras. Liman composed specific shots on set rather than capturing only raw data, because ASTEROID taught him that editing pure data without pre-selected shots is unworkable.
2. AI artists worked with the art department and production designer to generate environments as stills and frames.
3. Generated frames were fed into an animatic so Liman could evaluate in near-real-time whether scenes were working.
4. Scenes that were not working in the animatic were rewritten and reshot on stage.
5. Post-production: generated footage is assembled into scenes using the captured performances and composed shots as anchors. Witness cameras provide backup angles that Liman can choose to use in post if he changes his mind about a shot.

Jed Weintrob describes 30 Ninjas's production pipeline as explicitly agile: it changes every couple of weeks as new tools become available, unlike traditional VFX studio pipelines that are largely fixed. Gemini Omni was specifically credited with enabling the six-month post timeline.

segments.heading: ASTEROID: immersive VR film with AI interactive character extension
segments.text:
ASTEROID is a film shot in 180-degree stereoscopic for the Galaxy XR headset. The story involves a cast including DK Metcalf (NFL wide receiver, playing a version of himself) and other characters on an asteroid mission, most of whom do not survive. The film was directed by Liman and was made as part of a collaboration with the Android XR team.

After the film, Google approached 30 Ninjas about extending the story through an agentic interactive character. The extension: DK Metcalf's character, thought to be dead, turns out to be stranded on the asteroid. The viewer assumes the role of a NASA employee on Earth and must use voice conversation to help DK survive and be rescued.

Technically, the interactive character is built in Unity and uses the Gemini Live native audio API for natural language conversation. Julina Tatlock notes that Gemini Live native audio, which arrived approximately four months before the premiere, was the key capability that made natural conversational interaction possible rather than scripted NPC dialogue. The character is trained not just on DK Metcalf's real persona (he can discuss football, his career, and his personality) but specifically on DK-as-character-in-the-story (he knows he is stranded, has the stakes of the film's world).

Preparing the character required approximately 1,000 pages of writing to put the character through situations, establish behavioral guardrails, and define responses. For example: if a user tries to get DK to trash-talk other NFL players, the character diplomatically redirects. The writing process is substantial, not automated: the character requires a complete backstory, training, testing, and approval from DK Metcalf himself. Liman compares the interactive extension to sequels: instead of making a traditional sequel, the interactive chapter continues the story for audiences who want to stay in the world.

segments.heading: AI writing and jobs: the reality at 30 Ninjas
segments.text:
Mira Lane raises the question of whether AI is replacing screenwriters. The 30 Ninjas experience is the opposite: AI-driven expansion of scope creates more work, not less. Liman notes that many of his film industry peers are currently not working because the overall number of large productions has declined sharply. 30 Ninjas is hiring them: top film editors, screenwriters generating shot sequences for Bitcoin, an award-winning Brazilian feature film editor (since Brazil no longer finances large-budget films) who discovered AI tools and made AI shorts, was discovered at a festival by Tatlock, and is now a lead creative at 30 Ninjas. The company is also hiring AI-native artists alongside experienced filmmakers.

Weintrob is explicit: we are creating jobs, not generating them through AI. The expansion of scope in Bitcoin (150 locations, 125+ actors) created more casting and production work than a traditionally budgeted production would.

segments.heading: Advice for filmmakers working with AI tools
segments.text:
Jed Weintrob: Just go do it. Google and other companies have invested billions of dollars in tools that give any filmmaker access to capabilities previously unavailable. Use them. The best way to get hired at 30 Ninjas was to make AI shorts independently and be found through festivals.

Julina Tatlock: Learn what the tools do well, but also try to break them and make them produce results that look unlike everything else. AI video generation has recurring tendencies (subjects centered in frame, certain lighting patterns) that become stylistic fingerprints. Find the edges where the models fail in interesting ways and incorporate that into story and visual style deliberately. In Bitcoin, some scenes told in memory or from a past perspective lean into the specific visual qualities that AI generation produces.

Doug Liman: The advice is essentially the same as for traditional filmmaking: chart your own path, do not copy what exists, and do not use AI to skip the creative work. Using a language model to write a scene for you produces results that are terrible precisely because they are generic. The tools should amplify your humanity and your specific creative voice, not substitute for it.

title: Building a frontier AI search experience
description: Robby Stein, VP of Product for Google Search, joins host Logan Kilpatrick to explore how Search is evolving into a frontier AI product. Their conversation covers the shift from simple keywords to complex, conversational queries, the rise of agentic capabilities that can take action on your behalf, and the vision to help billions of users truly ask anything. Learn more about the technology behind AI Overviews, AI Mode, Deep Search, and the future of multimodal interaction.

segments.heading: Google Search as a frontier AI product: scale and mission
segments.text: Robby Stein (VP of Product for Google Search) and Logan Kilpatrick discuss the transformation of Google Search from a keyword index into a frontier AI product. Serving over 1.5 billion monthly users, Search represents the largest real-world deployment of Gemini models. The product vision centers on enabling users to ask open-ended questions of arbitrary complexity, synthesizing real-time web knowledge with deep contextual understanding.

segments.heading: AI Mode, query fan-out, and agentic search tooling
segments.text: Stein details the architecture behind AI Mode. Rather than processing inputs as single queries, AI Mode uses custom Gemini reasoning checkpoints to perform automated query fan-out: breaking multifaceted user questions into dozens of concurrent sub-queries. The model treats Google Search and real-time backend systems (such as the 50-billion-item Shopping Graph updated billions of times per hour and Google Finance tickers) as native tools before aggregating findings into an interactive synthesis.

segments.heading: Deep Search: multi-step research plans for high-stakes decisions
segments.text: For complex, high-stakes consumer queries (such as purchasing a fire-rated safe or evaluating college programs), Search provides Deep Search. Operating asynchronously in the background, Deep Search formulates structured research plans, explores hundreds of data sources across multiple minutes, evaluates technical specifications, and delivers comprehensive comparison dossiers complete with source citations and follow-up threads.

segments.heading: Visual search explosion: Google Lens and Circle to Search
segments.text: Multimodal visual queries represent Search's fastest-growing segment, expanding 70% year-over-year. Powered by Gemini's native vision architecture, tools like Google Lens and Circle to Search allow users to snap photos of physical objects (clothing, machinery, homework, or furniture) and execute follow-up refinement queries (e.g., asking for color variations or styling ideas) directly against Google's image corpus.

segments.heading: Search Live and real-time conversational assistance
segments.text: Stein introduces Search Live (developed in Google Labs), bringing low-latency conversational audio and live video into search. Users can point their smartphone cameras at real-world tasks (such as bicycle repairs or cooking recipes) while having a natural back-and-forth dialogue with Search, receiving real-time spoken guidance grounded in verified web links displayed directly in the viewfinder.

segments.heading: Personalization with privacy: integrating Gmail and user context
segments.text: Google Search is introducing opt-in personalization layers. By allowing models to access authorized user context (such as past purchases or travel itineraries via Gmail), Search eliminates redundant explanations for taste-dependent queries (e.g., autumn wardrobe recommendations or date-night dining). Factual and historical queries remain strictly neutral and objective.

segments.heading: Agentic execution: Project Mariner and the reality of task automation
segments.text: Stein explores the future of agentic search built on Gemini and Project Mariner. Rather than focusing solely on trivial end-point checkout buttons, agentic search solves high-friction discovery bottlenecks: continuously monitoring rolling calendar availability across hotel rooms or verifying seating configurations for concert tickets before handing the user a single verified confirmation step.

title: The future of software development
description: Coding is evolving from writing boilerplate to curating outcomes. Join the leads of Gemini, Google Antigravity, and Google AI Studio for a discussion on the rise of vibe coding and the agentic future of software development. Explore the reality of building with today's most advanced models, dive into the latest capabilities of Google's developer tools, and gain insights on how engineering roles are evolving.

segments.heading: Gemini 3.5 Flash: best model yet for agentic and long-running tasks
segments.text: Gemini 3.5 Flash outperforms Gemini 3.1 Pro on most benchmarks, with particular strength in tool use, long-running coding tasks, real-world finance tasks, productivity tasks like slide deck creation, and general multi-step reasoning. It combines high performance with high inference speed, publishing over 200 tokens per second, which is significantly faster than competing frontier models. The model is available via the API, in AI Studio, in the Gemini app, and in Antigravity. The meaning of Flash has shifted from a model for simple chat use cases to a model capable of extended agentic tasks. One demonstrated example: building an operating system through 15,000 model invocations.

segments.heading: Vibe coding versus agentic engineering: two distinct use cases
segments.text: The software development use case spans a spectrum. On one end, vibe coding: non-programmers building software for the first time, requiring high aesthetic quality and ease of iteration, lower verification requirements. On the other end, agentic engineering: professional developers building production systems, requiring the model to handle large legacy codebases, complex context, and multi-step orchestration with verifiable correctness. These two use cases require the same foundational model capabilities (reasoning, tool use, multimodal input, high-quality code generation) but differ in what they emphasize. Models need to see and be evaluated on both use case types to avoid excelling at one and failing at the other.

segments.heading: The product-model flywheel: why Antigravity is integral to training
segments.text: Varun Mohan describes how the Antigravity harness has become integral to model training, not just a consumer product. Early agent harnesses were simple (bash commands, file system calls, user prompts). Current Antigravity supports: native subagent creation, asynchronous parallel tool calls, the ability for users to override a running agent mid-task, and the model managing multiple concurrent tasks. These behavioral details cannot be learned purely from SWE-bench-style GitHub PR datasets. The team does reinforcement learning directly on real harness behavior. Researchers use Antigravity internally to experience the model's limitations, creating a direct feedback loop. This means benchmarks and product experience cannot be separated: a model that looks great on benchmarks but behaves poorly in the harness gets caught immediately because the same researchers are using both.

segments.heading: How to build products on a rapidly improving model foundation
segments.text: Michael Gerstenhaber identifies a key tension: every six months, models improve enough that the right product architecture changes. His advice: distinguish between failures because the model is not yet smart enough and failures because you built something wrong. Build for the former: design products that will work once the model improves, rather than workarounds that fight the model's strengths. The conversation around agents has already shifted from build me an agent to help me use your agent for my purpose, as pre-built agentic capabilities (agent API, agent CLI) often outperform what individual teams can build. He recommends thinking of the model as a coworker: same entity whether it reaches you via Slack, phone call, or email.

segments.heading: Where the bottleneck moves when coding is mostly solved
segments.text:
As models become increasingly capable at executing code from a clear specification, the bottlenecks move in two directions:

1. Upstream: what to build. When building is easy, the hard problem becomes identifying real user pain points and making hard calls about what features to ship. Varun Mohan emphasizes that high-agency product judgment, knowing what not to build, will be in short supply. You cannot add 100 buttons and expect users to benefit from all of them.

2. Downstream: information retrieval, deployment, and scaling. Gerstenhaber argues a significant current bottleneck is not intelligence but information retrieval: agents need access to real-time or sensitive data to complete tasks. Example: two banks running Know Your Customer compliance processes with AI agents only became possible after solving data credentialing, not after the model became smart enough. An SRE agent (diagnosing and fixing live production systems) is harder than a coding agent because it requires continuously querying live system state rather than working with static information already written down.

segments.heading: Benchmarks evolving toward product-like complexity
segments.text: Standard coding benchmarks are no longer adequate for measuring real-world model quality. Tulsee Doshi notes that internal evals are shifting toward approximating full product experiences. An external example is vending bench, which measures a model's ability to run a functional store and earn profit over multiple days. However, benchmarks are insufficient alone: a significant portion of developer feedback is qualitative and subjective even in coding, covering model tone, eagerness, laziness, and communication style during a task rather than just correctness of final output. Live experiments and side-by-side feedback are becoming essential complements to automated benchmarks.

segments.heading: Agent interface: when to interrupt, audio vs. visual, multi-agent orchestration
segments.text:
As agents run longer and more autonomously, the interface design problem shifts to: when should an agent interrupt a human, and with what channel? Gerstenhaber frames this as requiring agents to develop savoir-faire: knowing whether to ping immediately, wait an hour, or escalate. Getting this wrong leads to a persistently annoying agent rather than a useful coworker.

Mohan expects audio to become the dominant interaction modality for orchestrating multiple background agents, because voice is fast and allows interaction regardless of what surface you are on. He notes the open question of how to consume agent outputs, whether voice, text, or something else.

Doshi predicts a future where a single interface (potentially voice-driven) can spawn multiple specialized agents, replacing today's model of going to different apps for different tasks. This represents a major shift in product design principles.

For the question about model selection in multi-agent systems: the main agent in Antigravity can already choose which model (larger or smaller) to use for each subagent task. The direction of travel is large models delegating most subtasks to smaller models, reserving the large model for verification and judgment calls.

segments.heading: Avoiding AI slop: integration testing with agents
segments.text: Mohan's recommendation for avoiding regressions in AI-assisted codebases: from the very start of a project, set up the agent to spin up the application, navigate its UI, click buttons, and perform integration tests automatically. From those agent test runs, generate Playwright scripts of exactly what was clicked, then use those as persistent regression tests. He acknowledges this works best on greenfield projects. For existing products, some rearchitecting is required to enable this testing paradigm, which is substantial work.

title: Gemini co-leads on project origins and what's next
description: To mark the launch of Gemini 3.5 Flash, Logan Kilpatrick sat down at Gradient Canopy with four of the people who built it: Jeff Dean, Koray Kavukcuoglu, Noam Shazeer, and Oriol Vinyals. They talked about the origin of the Gemini project, the bet on a single unified model, why each Flash generation now outperforms the previous Pro, and what's coming next.

segments.heading: Origin of the Gemini project: merging fragmented teams
segments.text: Before Gemini started, multiple teams at Google Brain and DeepMind were independently building powerful models. Oriol Vinyals was leading efforts at DeepMind; Jeff Dean was steering work around the Pathways project, PaLM, and PaLM 2. Dean wrote a half-page internal memo arguing that fragmenting effort and compute across separate teams was counterproductive, and that building one single model jointly was the right approach. He credits the consolidation as the origin of the project name Gemini, meaning twins, representing the merger of the two organizations. Koray Kavukcuoglu noted the transition from an era of more academic-style AI research where parallelism was fine, to an era where each model training run requires massive concentrated effort across many researchers, making a focused single operation far more valuable than parallel teams.

segments.heading: Why product usage drives model improvement
segments.text: A key insight from the founders: having a model used at scale by real people is irreplaceable for understanding what is and is not working. Dean draws the analogy to Search, where usage statistics over many years revealed what needed improvement in ways that internal testing could not. Noam Shazeer adds that optimizing internally without real users risks hill-climbing benchmarks, including potentially contaminated ones, rather than building genuine capability. Kavukcuoglu frames it as: you cannot define the frontier of AI without simultaneously being at the frontier of product usefulness. Vinyals notes the bet was clear from the start: one powerful unified model would leap-frog everything Google was powering with separate ML models, even if the exact product shape was less obvious.

segments.heading: Gemini 3.5 Flash: distillation packing Pro capability into Flash
segments.text: Gemini 3.5 Flash is the focus of the conversation. Vinyals notes that each Flash generation has outperformed the previous generation's Pro model, and finds this consistently surprising given how much intelligence is packed per parameter. The mechanism is distillation: a large teacher model (the Pro) transfers knowledge to a smaller student model (Flash). The core technique from the original distillation paper (using soft labels from the teacher rather than hard labels from training data) is essentially unchanged, with modest tweaks. Kavukcuoglu summarizes it as squeezing the lemon: the juice (intelligence) comes out and goes into the glass (the smaller model). Jeff Dean clarifies the current approach: one very good teacher model and one student, no longer requiring the 50-model ensembles from the original research. The focus of Gemini 3.5 is on agentic and coding capabilities while maintaining and improving other capabilities.

segments.heading: Surprising progress: one box, general intelligence
segments.text: Shazeer reflects on an early Google philosophy called the one box: a single Search input box that users assumed was powered by a general-purpose AI behind the scenes, when in reality each result type (sports scores, stock quotes, weather) was a separate specialized backend. The ambition was always to build the actual general-purpose AI that the frontend implied. He says they have now built it. The user-facing interface is one box and there is finally one backend to match. This is framed as one of the biggest positive surprises of the Gemini project.

segments.heading: What has been harder than expected: evaluation and continual learning
segments.text:
On the challenging side, Vinyals identifies evaluation as consistently underappreciated. Evaluating model capabilities in ways that are not contaminated by training data, that users actually agree with, and that track what will be important next, remains a difficult unsolved problem. The field shifted from benchmark tables in papers to real user feedback, which itself introduced new complexity.

Dean expresses mild disappointment that continual learning and more organic, fluid model architectures (beyond today's MOE structure where all experts have similar structure) have not progressed further. He imagined more progress toward architectures with greater plasticity.

Kavukcuoglu observes that current models are not dramatically larger in parameter count than models from three or four years ago, yet they pack far more capability, suggesting there is still substantial untapped capacity that algorithmic improvements could unlock. Dean estimates LLMs need roughly 1,000 times more training data than humans to reach comparable capabilities, and believes that gap represents a major opportunity if algorithmic improvements can close it.

segments.heading: How the Gemini co-leads met each other
segments.text: Jeff Dean called Noam Shazeer in 2000 to persuade him to accept a Google offer; Shazeer joined and became Dean's officemate for three and a half years. Shazeer's starter project was the Did You Mean spell correction system in Search. Dean also called Oriol Vinyals in 2012 to persuade him to choose Google over a competing offer; Vinyals was finishing his PhD and joined to work on distillation, with Dean effectively acting as a coding assistant during the early implementation. Koray Kavukcuoglu's first significant interaction with Dean was during the DeepMind acquisition process in London, where Dean asked to review the DeepMind codebase directly alongside Kavukcuoglu during the due diligence process.

segments.heading: Gemini Omni and the world modeling direction
segments.text: Gemini Omni is a model that takes in any modality (text, image, audio, video, genomic sequences, chemical structure, robotic data, LiDAR) and outputs any modality, now including video generation. Kavukcuoglu distinguishes Omni from Veo (text-to-video) by arguing that a true world model must not only generate video but understand the dynamics, physics, and causality of the physical world well enough to simulate it forward, and to use those future simulations as the basis for decisions. That makes Omni a qualitatively different category from separate generation and understanding models. Vinyals notes that the joint training approach, where video, audio, text, and other modalities are trained together, is producing emergent capabilities like 3D consistency and scene coherence that previously required hand-specified rules, and that this seemed unlikely to work from first principles but has proven out at scale. Dean extends multimodality beyond human-centric modalities to scientific data types.

segments.heading: Predictions for I/O 2027: self-improvement and long-running agents
segments.text:
Kavukcuoglu predicts that by I/O 2027, models will be meaningfully contributing to their own improvement, with at least some significant Gemini capability having been generated by agents running experiments rather than by human researchers directly. Dean extends this: by then, the team will be able to point to specific model improvements that came from AI-directed self-improvement under human guidance.

Vinyals predicts continual learning will see meaningful progress: a model that can update its knowledge base through experience and interaction without requiring weight updates, so users see the model improving in real time based on what it has encountered.

Kilpatrick predicts a model that runs autonomously for 30 consecutive days becomes a demonstrated reality, which he sees as requiring the full stack: better memory systems, continual learning, and faster inference hardware (so 30 days of work compresses into one day of wall time). Dean adds that tool latency is an underappreciated constraint: most agent time is spent waiting for external tools built for human interaction cadences, not for model inference speed.

segments.heading: One model or thousands of products in five years
segments.text: Kavukcuoglu's answer: one product, the model. Google's current and future products are expressions of a single model becoming more capable. Dean qualifies this: there are many product interfaces and surfaces, each serving different human needs, but a smaller number of underlying capabilities that make all of them good. He cites the AI glasses demonstrated at I/O as a distinct product form from Search, both powered by the same underlying model. Vinyals notes that user intent segmentation (I want to check email, I want to buy something) may reflect a genuine human preference for separation of concerns rather than a technological limitation, and is cautious about predicting the consolidation away. Shazeer speculates that longer-term, physical products that move atoms rather than just bits may emerge from Omni-class models.

title: From prototype to production: 45 minutes to a reliable Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform agent
description: A production-first masterclass on building enterprise-grade agents with the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. Booking.com shares their evolution from LLM wrappers to a governed multi-provider platform running customer-facing and internal agents. Google engineers present the 4-step production framework: Connect (MCP servers), Protect (Model Armor, Agent Identity), Inspect (Cloud Tracing, Observability), and Perfect (Response & Trajectory Evals).

segments.heading: Booking.com case study: journey from wrappers to governed agent platform
segments.text: Booking.com processes 500,000 requests per second across 175,000 destinations. Engineering leaders Alibek Datbayev and Maria-Irène Călinoiu share their AI evolution: graduating from simple 2023 wrapper apps to a centralized internal gateway with unified governance, provisioning throughput for low latency, and shipping agents like 'Know Before You Go' (travel concierge), 'BigBot' (internal data mesh assistant), and 'Reels to Reality' (multimodal video itinerary planning).

segments.heading: Step 1: Connect via Model Context Protocol (MCP)
segments.text: Enterprise agents connect to real-world context using MCP servers. In the live London Travel Concierge demo, an orchestrator agent accesses real-time weather APIs and queries proprietary enterprise booking databases in Cloud SQL through standardized MCP tool interfaces, eliminating custom brittle integrations.

segments.heading: Step 2: Protect with Agent Identity and Model Armor
segments.text: Production deployments replace shared service accounts with discrete Agent Identities bound to least-privilege IAM roles. Model Armor sits in the data path, inspecting both user prompts for jailbreaks and tool outputs for sensitive PII exfiltration before tokens reach downstream applications.

segments.heading: Step 3 and 4: Inspect via Observability and Perfect via Trajectory Evaluations
segments.text: Observability provides forensic traces of tool execution lineages and latency bottlenecks. Quality is enforced using two-pronged evaluation: Response Evaluation (measuring groundedness and formatting) and Trajectory Evaluation (verifying intermediate tool calling logic, parameter validity, and step sequences against golden evaluation datasets via automated LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines).

title: Gemma 4 production stack: Model Armor, ADK Agents, Tracing
description: Step-by-step codelab on building a secure, observable Gemma 4 production agent stack on Google Cloud. Covers deploying open-weights Gemma 4 models on vLLM and Ollama on Cloud Run, securing traffic via Cloud Load Balancer with Model Armor Service Extensions (blocking prompt injection and PII leaks), scraping GPU metrics with a Prometheus sidecar, and instrumenting end-to-end OpenTelemetry Cloud Trace.

segments.heading: Architecture overview: securing and observing Gemma 4
segments.text: Building a production open-weights agent stack requires four core layers: (1) Optimized serving using vLLM and Ollama deployed on Cloud Run GPU instances, (2) Traffic routing through Cloud Load Balancing, (3) Security inspection via Model Armor service extensions, and (4) Comprehensive observability using Prometheus metrics and Cloud Trace.

segments.heading: Model security: Model Armor via Load Balancer Service Extensions
segments.text: Model Armor secures open-weights inference by intercepting both incoming prompts and outgoing completions. By deploying Model Armor as a Cloud Load Balancing Service Extension (running Envoy Callout filters), the security layer inspects payloads at the network edge, rejecting prompt injections, jailbreaks, and PII before requests touch the vLLM backend.

segments.heading: ADK Agent orchestration on Cloud Run
segments.text: The Agent Development Kit (ADK) wraps the Gemma 4 backend into an autonomous conversational agent. The agent is containerized and deployed to Cloud Run using automated Cloud Build CI/CD pipelines, supporting dynamic tool execution and session handling.

segments.heading: Observability: Prometheus metrics and end-to-end Cloud Trace
segments.text: Observability is implemented across two dimensions: a Prometheus sidecar container scrapes vLLM metrics (GPU memory utilization, token generation throughput, prefill latency), while OpenTelemetry traces propagate execution context through the ADK agent, database tools, and inference backends into Google Cloud Trace.

title: Generative UI for any agent, anywhere: A2UI, AG-UI, MCP Apps, and more
description: Explores the emergence of Generative UI standards to break beyond text-only chatbot walls. Details three complementary approaches: MCP Apps (interactive web UI extensions over Model Context Protocol), AG-UI from CopilotKit (bridging any frontend framework with agent backends), and A2UI (declarative data-driven UI treating design systems as secure trust catalogs) across Gemini Enterprise, Google Search, and the agentic web.

segments.heading: Breaking the chat wall: the evolution from text to adaptive interfaces
segments.text: Text-only chat interfaces create cognitive overload when presenting complex multi-dimensional data like funnel analytics, booking options, or financial charts. Generative UI dynamically generates interactive, brand-aligned graphical user interfaces in real time based on agent intent and user context.

segments.heading: MCP Apps: interactive frontend extensions over Model Context Protocol
segments.text: Ido Salomon explains MCP Apps, the official extension to MCP standardizing UI delivery from tool providers to client applications. When an agent queries an analytics server like PostHog, the server returns an interactive UI component (rendered in an isolated iframe or web component) rather than static text, allowing instant inline data exploration.

segments.heading: AG-UI by CopilotKit: universal agent-to-frontend bridge
segments.text: Atai Barkai presents AG-UI, an open-source protocol by CopilotKit that connects frontend application state with autonomous agent backends (LangChain, LangGraph, ADK, CrewAI). AG-UI enables bidirectional context sharing: agents can inspect frontend DOM/state and render dynamic generative widgets directly into native React/Vue components.

segments.heading: A2UI: declarative data-driven UI and design system trust catalogs
segments.text: Nicolas Le Pallec and Alan Blount introduce A2UI, Google's declarative UI standard. Instead of letting LLMs output arbitrary unsafe HTML/JavaScript, A2UI treats UI as structured JSON data referencing pre-approved enterprise design system components (the 'trust catalog'), guaranteeing strict visual consistency, mobile responsiveness, and zero XSS vulnerability.

title: Build a multi-agent system | Hands On AI (Part 1)
description: Part 1 of a hands-on multi-agent lab series using an RPG game theme. Covers setting up Google Cloud developer credits and APIs, building a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server to expose custom tools, and constructing specialized ADK workflow agents (Sequential Fire Familiar, Parallel Water Familiar, and Loop Earth Familiar) orchestrated by a central Summoner agent.

segments.heading: Hands-on project overview and multi-agent RPG architecture
segments.text: The codelab establishes a multi-agent RPG system where player commands are orchestrated by a Summoner agent coordinating specialized sub-agents: a Fire Familiar (sequential step execution), a Water Familiar (parallel data gathering), and an Earth Familiar (iterative validation loops). The architecture demonstrates modular tool and agent composition using ADK and MCP.

segments.heading: Building an MCP server for tool integration
segments.text: Developers create a custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) server using Python and FastAPI. The server exposes structured tools (calculating combat damage, querying spell registries, checking inventory state) with standardized JSON schemas that can be attached dynamically to any ADK agent.

segments.heading: Constructing specialized ADK workflow patterns
segments.text: The lab walks through coding distinct workflow agent topologies in ADK: (1) Sequential Agents executing deterministic linear pipelines, (2) Parallel Agents querying multiple sources concurrently to minimize latency, and (3) Loop / Evaluator Agents executing multi-turn validation loops until quality criteria are satisfied.

segments.heading: Orchestrating agents with the Summoner agent core
segments.text: The Summoner agent is configured with Gemini 2.5 Flash as its reasoning core. It parses freeform user intent, connects to the MCP tool server, delegates sub-tasks to the appropriate familiar agents, and synthesizes structured action plans ready for deployment in Part 2.

title: Build multi-agent AI A2A + Cloud Run | Hands On AI (Part 2)
description: Part 2 of the hands-on RPG multi-agent codelab series. Covers implementing the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol for direct distributed agent communication over HTTP, persisting memory and session state across multi-agent workflows, using agent lifecycle callbacks for guardrails and logging, containerizing agents with Cloud Build, and deploying the complete multi-agent cluster to Cloud Run for the final boss fight.

segments.heading: Distributed agent architecture and the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol
segments.text: While local workflow agents execute in-process, production architectures deploy agents as decoupled microservices across separate endpoints. The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol standardizes HTTP JSON messaging between remote agents, allowing the Summoner orchestrator to delegate combat and quest actions to remote Familiar agents running on independent Cloud Run services.

segments.heading: State management, memory persistence, and lifecycle callbacks
segments.text: The session integrates persistent state management to preserve inventory status, character stats, and multi-turn battle history. ADK lifecycle callbacks (e.g., before_tool_call, after_model_response) are implemented to enforce input guardrails, track token consumption, and log debug traces.

segments.heading: Containerization with Cloud Build and Artifact Registry
segments.text: Each agent microservice is packaged with Docker, built using Google Cloud Build, and published to Artifact Registry. Configuration variables (API keys, MCP endpoint URLs, model identifiers) are passed securely via environment parameters.

segments.heading: Deploying to Cloud Run and the final boss fight demo
segments.text: The complete multi-agent cluster is deployed to Google Cloud Run, utilizing serverless concurrency and automatic scaling. The lab concludes with a live RPG 'boss fight' where the Summoner and Familiar agents coordinate tactical spell selections, inventory updates, and iterative attack calculations in real time.

title: Indira Negi - Investing in AI hardware for health
description: Episode of the People of AI podcast featuring Indira Negi (Senior Advisor & Deputy Director at the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation). Traces her career from growing up in the Himalayan foothills to leading wearable sensor engineering at Intel, VP of Product at AliveCor, and funding breakthrough AI-powered medical hardware and handheld ultrasound devices to drastically reduce maternal and neonatal mortality in low-resource global communities.

segments.heading: From the Himalayas to biosensors: engineering for human impact
segments.text: Indira Negi shares her upbringing in Dehradun, India, and her academic journey studying electrical engineering and biosensors at Arizona State University. Her early work focused on developing electrochemical sensors to detect biomarkers, establishing a lifelong mission to eliminate human suffering through accessible medical technology.

segments.heading: Wearable sensors and ECG diagnostics: Intel and AliveCor
segments.text: Negi spent over a decade at Intel leading sensor engineering for wearable devices and advising Intel Capital on health investments. She later joined AliveCor as VP of Product Management, pioneering smartphone-connected FDA-cleared electrocardiogram (ECG) hardware that brought clinical cardiac monitoring into patients' pockets.

segments.heading: Gates Foundation mission: AI hardware for maternal and newborn health
segments.text: In 2021, Negi established the Devices and AI team within the Maternal, Newborn & Child Health Discovery program at the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. In low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), preventable pregnancy and childbirth complications remain leading causes of mortality due to extreme shortages of trained sonographers and diagnostic equipment.

segments.heading: AI-enabled ultrasound and the future of clinical AI assistance
segments.text: The foundation invests in low-cost handheld ultrasound probes paired with on-device computer vision models. The AI guides untrained frontline community health workers in real time to position the probe correctly and automatically measures gestational age, detects fetal anomalies, and flags obstetric risks. Negi discusses the promise and pitfalls of clinical AI chatbots, emphasizing rigorous safety and cultural adaptation.

title: Intent-driven development with Claude Code and Fable 5
description: Are you still writing your software architecture line by line, or are you letting autonomous agents do the heavy lifting? In this episode of The Agent Factory, we explore the radical shift toward intent-driven development, where your job is to tell the AI what to build rather than how to build it. Host Smitha Kolan sits down with Lydia Hallie from Anthropic and YK Sugi, the creator of CS Dojo and author of the viral Claude Code Tips repository.

segments.heading: Intent-driven development: expressing what, not how
segments.text: YK Sugi coined intent-driven development as distinct from prompt-engineering advice. The principle is knowing exactly what you want to build and expressing that intent clearly, rather than specifying implementation steps. One concrete tip: use voice-to-type instead of keyboard typing. Voice allows faster, less self-censored expression of intent. Lydia Hallie (Anthropic) notes the team internally focuses on verification as a core part of intent: plan mode, adding images, and using structured prompts that give Claude context on what the developer actually wants.

segments.heading: Claude Code at enterprise scale via Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
segments.text: Claude Code runs locally by default but can be pointed at Google Cloud's Vertex AI backend for enterprise-scale deployment. Setup: install gcloud SDK, set Project ID from Cloud Console, enable Vertex AI API, set environment variables for Vertex AI integration, then start Claude. Alternatively, the built-in setup-vertex wizard handles most steps automatically: it checks application default credentials, selects a project, runs a quick haiku-level model check, and lists available models including Opus 46 and Fable 5.

segments.heading: Demo: building a 3D slingshot game via voice prompts
segments.text: YK demonstrated intent-driven development by building a 3D physics slingshot game using Three.js and ammo wrap (a physics library). The workflow: start broad (what architecture and libraries to use, asking Claude to suggest options), then iterate narrower (add trajectory preview, then shatter targets). Claude autonomously ran Playwright tests it was not asked to run. YK prompted entirely by voice. The game was committed to a public GitHub repository via Claude, with a draft PR created automatically using Claude's GitHub CLI integration.

segments.heading: Auto Mode: the solution to permission fatigue
segments.text: Permission fatigue occurs when Claude Code asks confirmation for every action, causing users to approve without reading. The previous bypass option was skipping permissions entirely, which is dangerous. Auto Mode sits between the two: it runs a classifier on each tool call to assess danger. If the tool call is clearly dangerous (deleting an unexpected file), it asks. If it is a routine read, edit, or write the user implicitly approved by initiating the task, it proceeds silently. Auto Mode is also more resistant to prompt injection because the classifier catches instructions embedded in tool outputs.

segments.heading: Dynamic Workflows: parallel subagents with a JavaScript plan file
segments.text: Dynamic Workflows is a Claude Code feature invoked by natural language: the phrase use a dynamic workflow causes Claude to generate a structured JavaScript workflow file. That file defines named build phases (for example, build-engine, build-UI, build-audio, build-haptics) that run in parallel, followed by sequential integration, review, and verify phases. The workflow can be saved with a name and re-run deterministically. Individual subagents within the workflow can be configured to use different models (for example, cheaper Sonnet for low-complexity agents, Fable 5 for complex ones). Lydia ran the demo on Fable 5.

segments.heading: The software engineer role is shifting toward product manager
segments.text: Lydia Hallie frames the shift: with Claude Code generating most code, the engineer's role moves toward understanding architecture, owning feature intent, and reviewing output. The analogy: just as machine code once mattered but engineers now focus on higher-level abstractions, engineers are moving from writing syntax to owning architecture and taste. The review ratio has inverted: previously 90% writing, 10% reviewing; now 90% reviewing, 10% hand-coding. YK adds that engineers must remain responsible for output and not commit generated code blindly.

segments.heading: Claude Code as a universal computer interface
segments.text: YK uses Claude Code for video editing, data analysis, storage cleanup, research, and real estate research. He used it to compile a list of realtor email addresses when buying a property, saving him roughly $10,000 in commission. The terminal is returning as the universal interface to the computer. Lydia notes that internally at Anthropic, non-engineering teams (marketing, data science) started using Claude Code for non-coding tasks, which led the team to build Claude Cowork: a desktop app that uses the same runtime but has better connectors and system prompts for non-technical tasks like email, calendar management, and booking.

segments.heading: Craft, technical debt, and the Hacker News debate
segments.text: A recurring debate on Hacker News argues that AI coding tools reduce craft and increase technical debt. YK's position: the engineer is responsible for the output, not the tool. Just as a painter using an automated brush is still accountable for the painting, engineers should not commit generated code they have not verified. The solution is drafting PRs, reviewing manually or with AI before merging. Lydia notes that having Claude-bot enabled on GitHub means it automatically attempts to fix CI failures and reviewer comments by pushing to the branch, which compresses the review loop.

title: The Impossible Computing with Keith Ballinger | The Agent Factory Podcast
description: Episode of The Agent Factory Podcast featuring Keith Ballinger. Explores 'Impossible Computing' - building software and agentic workflows that were previously economically or computationally infeasible. Discusses developer leverage, Gemini CLI, multimodal media pipelines (Veo 3, Imagen 4), and moving from basic coding assistance to autonomous agents executing multi-step production deployments on Cloud Run.

segments.heading: Impossible computing: rethinking software economics with AI
segments.text: Keith Ballinger introduces 'Impossible Computing' - the concept that modern foundation models make previously unthinkable software applications economically viable to build overnight. Tasks requiring months of manual coding or complex heuristics can now be solved with high-leverage agentic prompts and autonomous tooling.

segments.heading: Developer empowerment and the shift to vibe coding
segments.text: The hosts discuss how agentic IDEs and Gemini CLI transform the developer experience. Software development evolves from writing manual syntax line-by-line to orchestrating high-level architectural intent, rapid prototyping, and automated iterative debugging.

segments.heading: Multimodal media generation pipelines: Veo 3 and Imagen 4
segments.text: The conversation explores chaining reasoning models with multimodal generation tools like Veo 3 for cinematic video and Imagen 4 for high-resolution graphics. Agents synthesize unstructured concepts, script narrative scenes, and dynamically call generative media APIs to produce interactive media applications.

segments.heading: Deploying production agents to Cloud Run
segments.text: Ballinger highlights architectural patterns for deploying agents into production. Utilizing serverless container platforms like Cloud Run allows developer agents to handle spiky user traffic with instant elasticity, low idle costs, and robust API governance.

title: Keras Turns 10: A decade of deep learning
description: Celebrate 10 years of Keras! In this special anniversary interview, Developer Advocate Yufeng Guo sits down with Keras founder François Chollet and engineer Matt Watson to discuss the library's incredible decade-long journey.

segments.heading: The origin of Keras: from Theano chatbot tooling to open-source library
segments.text: François Chollet recounts founding Keras in early 2015. While building a question-answering chatbot research project (an early precursor to RAG) using Theano, Chollet developed reusable tooling for Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and LSTMs. Frustrated by the complexity of existing 2014-era machine learning tooling (which required brittle YAML config files like Caffe), he packaged the components into a user-friendly library modeled on scikit-learn's ergonomics and released it on GitHub under the domain Keras.io.

segments.heading: Etymology: the Gate of Horn from Homer's Odyssey
segments.text: Chollet explains the literary origin of the name Keras (Greek for horn). In Homer's Odyssey, dreams visit Earth through two portals: false, deceptive dreams pass through a gate of polished ivory (elephas, sounding like elephairo, to deceive), while true, prophetic visions pass through the Gate of Horn (keras, sounding like kraino, to fulfill). Keras was conceived as the portal through which true visions of the AI future could be realized, maintaining thematic Greek naming consistency with Theano.

segments.heading: Evolution of Keras versions: 0.x to 3.0
segments.text:
The framework traversed several distinct architectural eras:

- Keras 0.x (2015): Sequential API centered on RNNs, LSTMs, and ConvNets on Theano, quickly adding multi-backend support when TensorFlow launched in late 2015.
- Keras 1.0 (2016): Introduced the Functional API, customizable callbacks, metrics, and losses.
- Keras 2.0 (2017-2018): Tight integration into TensorFlow (tf.keras), dropping multi-backend support due to organizational pressure.
- Keras 3.0 (2023+): Rebuilt from scratch in two months as a standalone, framework-agnostic system supporting JAX, PyTorch, TensorFlow, NumPy, OpenVINO, and MLX without requiring a TensorFlow installation.

segments.heading: Design philosophy: progressive disclosure of complexity
segments.text: The enduring architectural principle behind Keras is progressive disclosure of complexity: simple, standard workflows must require only 2 to 20 lines of clean code, while advanced customizations remain possible through incremental adjustments without hitting architectural cliffs. Developers can start with high-level Sequential models, customize layer logic via sub-classing, or descend directly into native framework kernels (such as custom JAX or PyTorch operations).

segments.heading: Pre-trained models, KerasHub, and Kaggle integration
segments.text: Matt Watson discusses how ML workflows have evolved from training models from scratch to fine-tuning large pre-trained foundation models. KerasCV and KerasNLP have consolidated into KerasHub, a unified library for text, vision, and multimodal architectures (including Stable Diffusion and LLMs). KerasHub integrates natively with Kaggle Models for hosting open weights, allowing seamless deployment across Colab, Kaggle Notebooks, and local scripts.

segments.heading: Kaggle's role in ML best practices
segments.text: Chollet and Watson emphasize Kaggle as a crucible for practical machine learning advances. Chollet competed in Kaggle's 2014 Higgs Boson challenge (placing 4th), which popularized XGBoost and gradient-boosted decision trees. Kaggle competitions provide an empirical, hype-free benchmark for identifying architectures and libraries that deliver verifiable performance on real-world datasets.

segments.heading: Advice for ML practitioners: first principles over hype cycles
segments.text: Chollet and Watson advise developers navigating AI hype. While weekly headlines generate noise, underlying deep learning theory, core model architectures (transformers, RNNs, backpropagation), and training dynamics remain remarkably stable over multi-year horizons. Practitioners should learn foundational concepts thoroughly (e.g., via Deep Learning with Python) and evaluate new papers and techniques from first principles rather than social media momentum.

segments.heading: The next 10 years: program synthesis and neuro-symbolic AI
segments.text: Looking ahead to 2035, Chollet anticipates the primary growth frontier in AI will be program synthesis and the fusion of deep learning with symbolic reasoning (autonomous discrete program search and learning symbolic representations). Both speakers predict that core deep learning abstractions and differentiable optimization will remain foundational to software development for decades to come.

title: Koray Kavukcuoglu: This Is How We Are Going to Build AGI
description: Join Logan Kilpatrick and Koray Kavukcuoglu, CTO of Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect of Google, as they discuss Gemini 3 and the state of AI! Their conversation includes the reception of Gemini 3, the ongoing advancements in AI research, and the role of benchmarks in pushing new frontiers. They explore critical areas for Gemini's focus, emphasizing instruction following, tool calls, and internationalization, alongside Google's collaborative approach to AI development.

segments.heading: Gemini 3 launch reception and continuous research acceleration
segments.text: Koray Kavukcuoglu (CTO of Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect of Google) reflects on the global release of Gemini 3. Contrasting the prevailing external skepticism about model scaling limits, Kavukcuoglu asserts that research momentum across pre-training, post-training, and reinforcement learning has accelerated rather than plateaued. When static benchmarks (such as GPQA Diamond) near saturation, new dynamic evaluations (HLE, ARC-AGI-2) emerge to measure newly unlocked reasoning frontiers.

segments.heading: Key focus areas for Gemini: instruction following, internationalization, and tool calls
segments.text:
Kavukcuoglu identifies the core capabilities prioritized in Gemini 3:

1. Instruction following: Ensuring models adhere precisely to user constraints rather than hallucinating generic responses.
2. Internationalization: Expanding multilingual reasoning depth for non-English languages historically underserved by frontier LLMs.
3. Function calling and agentic code generation: Empowering models to naturally invoke external APIs, author their own tools, and write functional software to solve digital tasks.

segments.heading: Product scaffolding: Antigravity, AI Studio, and real-world signal
segments.text: Kavukcuoglu emphasizes that artificial general intelligence will not be constructed in isolated research silos. Google's product ecosystem (Antigravity coding harness, AI Studio, Gemini App, and Search AI Mode) provides high-bandwidth user feedback loops. Direct signals from professional developers and enterprise users allow model researchers to identify behavioral bottlenecks and optimize training runs for real-world utility rather than theoretical benchmarks.

segments.heading: Role of Chief AI Architect: aligning research with global products
segments.text: In his dual role as DeepMind CTO and Google Chief AI Architect, Kavukcuoglu bridges frontier research with massive-scale product deployment. Rather than dictating product features, the architecture team provides foundational models and frameworks to internal Google product teams, synchronizing Day 1 global launches across billions of touchpoints while maintaining rigorous engineering standards for safety and security.

segments.heading: From pure research to an engineering mindset: scaling DeepMind
segments.text: Kavukcuoglu charts the cultural evolution of DeepMind. Historically focused on academic paper publishing (DQN, AlphaGo, AlphaFold), the organization transitioned into an engineering discipline shipping major model families every six months and minor iterations every 45 days. Research teams now organize around shared mainlines (such as Deep Think competing in IMO and ICPC) while maintaining exploratory scientific freedom.

segments.heading: Generative media convergence: Nano Banana and Nano Banana Pro
segments.text: The panel discusses the unification of text and vision architectures. From early PixelCNN experiments to Nano Banana and Nano Banana Pro (built on Gemini 3 Pro), generative media models have merged with multimodal foundation models. Rather than operating as isolated diffusion systems, unified architectures comprehend complex multimodal inputs (such as synthesizing dense technical documents into precise infographics) through joint world representations.

segments.heading: Google's comeback story and the imperative of ongoing innovation
segments.text: Kavukcuoglu recounts joining DeepMind in 2012 as its first deep learning researcher out of Yann LeCun's NYU lab. He candidly acknowledges that Google experienced an underdog phase when modern LLMs first surged, requiring the company to catch up on large language model training. Rather than relying solely on infrastructure scale, Google regained its leadership position (crossing 1500 Elo on the LMSYS Arena with Gemini 3) through relentless algorithmic innovation across the entire vertical stack.

title: Engineering the future of Kubernetes for AI at scale
description: Deep dive into Kubernetes architecture engineered for large-scale AI inference and autonomous agent workloads. Traces the evolution from stateless containers ('cattle') and StatefulSets to AI-native scheduling, Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA), Kueue batch management, and hardware-aware topology routing. Features Palo Alto Networks sharing their enterprise GKE AI infrastructure.

segments.heading: Evolution of Kubernetes: from stateless cattle to AI accelerators
segments.text: Kaslin Fields outlines the historical arc of Kubernetes: beginning with stateless ephemeral containers ('cattle, not pets'), introducing StatefulSets for persistent databases in 2016, and now transforming into an AI-first orchestrator optimizing specialized TPU, GPU, and memory accelerator topologies.

segments.heading: Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) and Kueue batch queuing
segments.text: AI workloads require granular control over specialized accelerator hardware. Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) standardizes driver-level GPU/TPU slicing and interconnect visibility, while open-source Kueue manages multi-tenant job queues, fair-share scheduling, and automated preemption across large-scale model training and inference clusters.

segments.heading: GKE Agent Sandbox and infrastructure fluidity for AI agents
segments.text: Jago Macleod details how GKE supports autonomous AI agent execution. Using gVisor kernel sandboxing, GKE spins up isolated code-execution pods in subseconds, providing total compute and network isolation for untrusted agent-generated code with snapshot-based suspend/resume to minimize idle compute costs.

segments.heading: Enterprise case study: Palo Alto Networks on GKE
segments.text: Boaz Rant from Palo Alto Networks explains how their cybersecurity platform scales AI inference across global GKE clusters. By leveraging automated node auto-provisioning and Kueue scheduling, they run real-time threat detection models with 99.99% availability and optimized accelerator utilization.

title: Agents, AI & The Next Wave: Mike Clark on Vertex AI at DevFest Silicon Valley
description: AI just reset the developer playbook. In this DevFest Silicon Valley sit-down, Mike Clark (Google Director of Product Management, AI Agents) sits down with Frank (Puf) Van Puffelen (Google Developer Expert and Engineer), sharing how agents are moving from demos to production with Vertex AI Agent Builder, Agent Engine, and the open-source Agent Developer Kit (SDK). They also discuss what build scale govern means for real teams.

segments.heading: DevFest energy and the democratizing reset of AI
segments.text: Mike Clark (Director of Product Management for AI Agents at Google Cloud) and Frank van Puffelen discuss the atmosphere at DevFest Silicon Valley. Clark highlights that modern generative AI represents a global reset across engineering, product management, and research disciplines. Unlike earlier computational eras requiring massive capital and specialized supercomputing access, modern agent platforms make advanced tools accessible to individual builders, startups, and enterprises alike.

segments.heading: Shifting from syntax mastery to creative intent and business outcomes
segments.text: Clark and van Puffelen reflect on historical shifts in software engineering (from early Unix, Photobucket, and early Firebase client-side databases to modern vibe coding). Historically, developers had to master low-level syntax, dependency management, and specific language dialects before solving problems. Today, creativity and architectural intent matter as much as manual coding chops. Citizen creators build functional software using tools like AI Studio and ADK, while marketing and product teams deploy substantial volumes of functional business logic without traditional engineering bottlenecks.

segments.heading: Rethinking code quality: outcome-driven evaluation vs. traditional PRs
segments.text: The speakers discuss how code quality is evaluated in agentic ecosystems. Clark argues that businesses measure success by outcomes (whether a system securely, reliably, and safely achieves its intended business goal) rather than stylistic code perfection. The concept of the traditional pull request is evolving into continuous agent validation loops where multi-step autonomous agents verify intermediate safety, security, and functional boundaries at every execution step.

segments.heading: Vertex AI Agent Platform: ADK, Agent Engine, and runtime hosting
segments.text:
Clark details the core architecture of Google Cloud's agent stack:

1. Agent Development Kit (ADK): An open-source framework for orchestrating models, instructions, and tools.
2. Agent Engine: A fully managed runtime providing scalable hosting, identity authentication, execution traces, observability (built on OpenTelemetry), and evaluation frameworks.
3. Deployment flexibility: Agents developed with ADK can deploy natively to Vertex AI Agent Engine, Google Cloud Run, or custom GKE clusters, powering internal Google products and enterprise suites like Gemini Enterprise.

segments.heading: The Build-Scale-Govern lifecycle for enterprise agents
segments.text: Clark frames the evolution of enterprise agent adoption across three distinct phases: Build (initial prototype exploration and prompt engineering), Scale (deploying high-concurrency runtimes with telemetry and performance tracing), and Govern (enforcing granular RBAC security, agent identity authentication, and regulatory compliance). Case study: Color Health leverages the full stack to build regulated healthcare workflows for cancer screening adherence while complying with strict healthcare governance mandates.

segments.heading: Open standards: A2A, A2UI, A2P, and Linux Foundation contributions
segments.text:
To foster interoperability across the industry, Google Cloud open-sources core agentic protocols and contributes them to the Linux Foundation:

- A2A (Agent-to-Agent): Standardizing direct inter-agent communication, discovery, and skill negotiation.
- A2UI (Agent-to-UI): Standardizing dynamic real-time user interface generation from agent streams.
- A2P (Agent-to-Payment): Establishing protocols for secure agentic transactions and commercial contracts.

title: The evolved developer with Muhammad Farooq
description: Meet Muhammad Farooq, a machine learning engineer and YouTuber (@engineerprompt), as he discusses RAG architectures, localGPT 2.0 development, transitioning to a technical manager mindset with AI coding agents, and best practices for specs-driven development.

segments.heading: Academic roots and the viral launch of engineerprompt
segments.text: Muhammad Farooq (PhD machine learning engineer and creator of the @engineerprompt YouTube channel with over 200,000 subscribers) recounts his transition from biomedical sensor research to AI education. When ChatGPT launched in late 2022, Farooq began recording technical video demos to explain LLM mechanisms to friends. An early tutorial on AI avatars went viral with over a million views in its first week, prompting him to establish a dedicated educational channel focused on hands-on open-source machine learning.

segments.heading: RAG fundamentals and enterprise search systems
segments.text: Farooq explains the architectural necessity of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Foundation models are frozen at pre-training cutoffs and lack access to proprietary enterprise data. RAG functions as an intelligent search substrate: it exposes private, dynamic business context to capable models, allowing autonomous agents to synthesize up-to-date reports, answer queries, and execute downstream workflows without requiring expensive model retraining.

segments.heading: Building LocalGPT: from weekend project to LocalGPT 2.0
segments.text: Farooq created LocalGPT, an open-source private RAG framework with over 21,000 GitHub stars, allowing privacy-conscious enterprises to run air-gapped document search on local hardware without sending data to third-party APIs. Building the initial version required manual implementation on raw llama.cpp bindings and NVIDIA drivers. For LocalGPT 2.0, modern runtimes (Ollama, vLLM, Apple MLX) and AI coding assistants enabled rapid cross-platform support, complete test coverage, and polished full-stack frontends.

segments.heading: The developer as technical manager: specs-driven iterative development
segments.text: Farooq describes how AI coding tools transform the software developer's role from writing syntax to functioning as a technical manager. To prevent models from implementing poorly optimized tech stacks or hallucinating unwanted features, developers must practice specs-driven development: writing rigorous product requirement specifications, decomposing systems into focused subtasks, and executing incremental, multi-shot feature builds with continuous manual code review.

segments.heading: Failure modes of agentic coding: forgotten context and silent regressions
segments.text: Farooq identifies subtle failure modes in AI-generated software. As codebases grow, agents can suffer from context fragmentation: reimplementing duplicate features they previously built or modifying function signatures across some call sites while silently missing others. Additionally, overly agreeable models rarely challenge flawed architectural choices. Developers must maintain deep system comprehension and enforce rigorous automated test suites rather than blindly trusting one-shot code generation.

segments.heading: The primacy of data engineering over algorithmic magic
segments.text: Farooq cautions against neglecting foundational data quality. In production RAG systems, developers frequently cycle through arbitrary chunking heuristics rather than inspecting their source documents. Structuring chunks around natural document semantics (such as sections, abstracts, and table layouts) dramatically improves retrieval accuracy and reduces overall pipeline complexity.

segments.heading: Model selection: Gemini long context and tiered Pro-Flash workflows
segments.text: Farooq discusses practical LLM deployment patterns. Gemini's 1-million-token context window provides essential global codebase understanding for complex multi-file refactoring. In multi-agent architectures, Farooq advocates a tiered approach: employing Gemini 2.5 Pro as an architectural planner to design specifications, while delegating high-throughput code implementation and testing to low-latency, cost-effective models like Gemini Flash.

title: Build a multi-agent system: A2A and Agent Registry
description: When you have 100 AI agents across your org, how do they find and talk to each other? This episode of Hands On AI covers Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol and Agent Registry. Build a production-ready multi-agent system: start with A2A (HTTP for AI agents), then solve agent sprawl with Agent Registry so your agents discover each other instead of hard-coding URLs. Built live with a dog walker agent and a trip planner agent using Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK), then orchestrated together.

segments.heading: What is Agent2Agent (A2A): HTTP for AI agents
segments.text: A2A (Agent to Agent) protocol is Google's open protocol for inter-agent communication, announced in 2025. The analogy: just as HTTP lets any browser talk to any web server regardless of the server software, A2A lets agents built with any framework (ADK, LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI) discover and communicate with each other. Agents expose an agent card at /.well-known/agent-card.json: a JSON file describing their name, description, capabilities, and the URL to connect to them. This serves as the agent's LinkedIn profile or business card.

segments.heading: When to use A2A vs. local sub-agents
segments.text: ADK supports local sub-agents (sequential and workflow agents) that run in-process. A2A is preferred when agents need to run remotely and independently, when loose coupling is required for easier maintenance and independent deployment, or when agents are built by different teams or with different frameworks. Without A2A, each inter-agent connection requires custom HTTP endpoints, custom authentication, and hardcoded URLs. With A2A, all of this is standardized and agents can be updated independently without redeploying the entire system.

segments.heading: Synchronous vs. asynchronous A2A communication
segments.text: A2A supports two communication modes. Synchronous polling: the client agent repeatedly calls the remote agent to check for results (analogous to standing in a bubble tea shop repeatedly asking if the order is ready). Streaming with Server-Sent Events (SSE): the client subscribes to the remote agent and receives push notifications when results are available (analogous to getting a push notification when the order is ready). Both modes can be configured in A2A.

segments.heading: Demo: wrapping an ADK agent as an A2A remote agent
segments.text: The dog walker agent is a standard ADK LLM agent using Gemini Flash with four tools: get_dog_profile, get_local_weather, find_park, and find_walk_route. Wrapping it as an A2A remote agent requires adding to_a2a from the ADK library in a server.py file. The agent card is either auto-generated or customized with skills metadata. Once wrapped, the agent serves a JSON agent card at /.well-known/agent-card.json. A trip planner agent on the client side connects to the dog walker by reading its agent card URL and calling it via A2A. This requires only the agent card URL to be known at design time.

segments.heading: Agent sprawl and why Agent Registry solves it
segments.text: Agent sprawl occurs when an organization has many agents (tens to hundreds) spread across cloud, on-premises, and hybrid environments. Problems: no central inventory of what agents exist or who owns them, each agent requires custom connection logic, no governance or auditability. Agent Registry solves three problems: (1) reusability, agents and MCP servers are registered once and discoverable by any agent in the organization; (2) standardized connectivity, one way to connect to any registered agent, MCP server, or endpoint regardless of their implementation; (3) governance and audit, cloud-native audit compliance, cost tracking, and risk monitoring in a central view. Agent Registry is not limited to ADK: LangGraph, CrewAI, and agents hosted in other clouds or on-premises can all be registered.

segments.heading: Registering agents via gcloud and Cloud Console
segments.text: Agents are registered using either the gcloud CLI command (which passes an agent card JSON to create a new Agent Registry service entry) or the Cloud Console UI (paste-from-JSON flow). After registration, the console shows each agent's ID, protocol (A2A), and skills. Google Cloud's own MCP servers are pre-populated in Agent Registry and can be discovered and enabled from the console. Agent policies (currently in private preview) allow administrators to restrict which agents or MCP servers a given agent is permitted to call.

segments.heading: Connecting through Agent Registry instead of hardcoded URLs
segments.text: Agent Registry exposes an MCP server. Instead of hardcoding agent URLs in orchestrator code, the orchestrator connects to the Agent Registry MCP server, passes tags or descriptions in a prompt, and the registry dynamically returns the URL for the correct agent or MCP tool. The returned URL is then used to make the A2A call. This eliminates hardcoded URLs and allows the system to scale as new agents are added without code changes. The same pattern works for MCP tool discovery: the orchestrator uses the registry to dynamically find and call MCP servers.

segments.heading: Demo: orchestrator agent using Agent Registry (dog walker plus trip planner)
segments.text: The orchestrator agent sends a single prompt (walk Bobby this afternoon and plan a two-day trip to Lisbon) to the sequential ADK agent. The agent calls the Agent Registry MCP server to search for the registered dog walker and trip planner agents, gets back their IDs and URLs, and then uses call_remote_agent to make A2A calls to each. The result combines a trip summary with a pet care routine. The same orchestrator pattern can be extended so that sub-agents (dog walker, trip planner) themselves query the registry to discover and call MCP tools like Google Maps dynamically.

segments.heading: Authentication in A2A and Agent Registry
segments.text: Agent Registry and A2A use Google Application Default Credentials by default. Agents authenticating with gcloud auth login or service accounts use those credentials. For user-delegated credentials (three-legged OAuth), the access token must be fetched and refreshed separately, then passed to the agent. User-credential flows with OAuth will be covered in a future episode.

title: How to design a multi-agent system that skips the LLM
description: Architectural deep dive into 'Race Condition' - a 1,000-agent marathon simulation built on Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) where almost none of the agents call the LLM. Casey West breaks down when to delegate decisions to LLMs vs. deterministic code, using the before_model_callback trick to bypass model inference, the NP-hard Spine & Sprout route planning algorithm, and scaling 1,000 stateless agents on Redis.

segments.heading: The core architectural dilemma: LLM reasoning vs. deterministic code
segments.text: Many AI engineers mistakenly route every micro-decision through expensive LLM inference. In 'Race Condition', a simulation of 1,000 marathon runners, only the initial course design and runner persona formulation require LLM creativity. Running continuous physics, pacing calculations, and route waypoints via LLMs would cost millions of wasted tokens with high latency.

segments.heading: The before_model_callback technique: keep the agent, skip the model
segments.text: The ADK provides a before_model_callback hook that inspects incoming user and agent state before firing an LLM inference call. If the required action can be calculated deterministically (e.g., checking runner stamina, updating coordinates), the callback computes the result directly and short-circuits the pipeline with an immediate structured response, consuming 0 tokens.

segments.heading: Deterministic pathfinding: NP-hard route planning and the Spine & Sprout algorithm
segments.text: Generating an exact 26.2-mile marathon course passing required cultural waypoints is an NP-hard graph traversal problem. Rather than asking an LLM to hallucinate map coordinates, the system pairs high-level LLM waypoint selection with a deterministic 'Spine & Sprout' graph algorithm that mathematically constructs optimal road routes.

segments.heading: Scaling 1,000 stateless agent sessions with Redis
segments.text: To scale 1,000 autonomous runner agents executing concurrent tick loops, the architecture decouples agent execution from persistent storage. Runner state (pace, hydration, fatigue, position) is maintained in Redis, allowing lightweight worker processes to resume and tick agents statelessly without memory overhead.

title: Building the quantum-AI future with Hartmut Neven and James Manyika
description: Join Hartmut Neven and James Manyika to explore the intersection of quantum computing and AI. Discover how AI is helping to build and operate quantum computers, while quantum unlocks new ways for AI models to train, learn from complex data, and accelerate scientific discovery, making quantum a key part of Google’s innovation strategy.

segments.heading: Quantum computing fundamentals and superposition
