segments.text: Hartmut Neven explains that the computational advantage of quantum computers originates in superposition: quantum physics states that a system can exist simultaneously in many configurations that evolve together in time. On Google's Willow chip, 105 physical qubits can exist in a superposition of 2^105 distinct bit strings. In a single clock cycle, the processor can interact with 2^105 states simultaneously, enabling calculations that would take the largest classical supercomputers 10 septillion years to complete. Macroscopic superconducting circuits (using Josephson junctions and aluminum loops cooled to 10 millikelvin) create artificial atoms that exhibit quantized energy levels while remaining engineerable at chip scale.

segments.heading: Hardware progress: coherence times and cooling
segments.text: Keeping quantum states alive requires extending coherence time (the duration superpositions survive without decaying into classical noise). Coherence times on Google chips have advanced from 20 microseconds to over 250 microseconds, shifting the primary engineering bottleneck from basic quantum physics limits to system-level integration and control electronics. The processor operates at 10 millikelvin in dilution refrigerators because temperature represents thermal noise that destroys delicate quantum states.

segments.heading: Feynman's killer app and quantum simulation targets
segments.text: Neven emphasizes that quantum computers are specialized accelerators rather than general-purpose replacements for classical machines. Their premier application, envisioned by Richard Feynman, is simulating quantum systems where combinatorial complexity defeats classical computers. Specific practical targets include designing lithium-air batteries (which offer higher theoretical energy density than jet kerosene, potentially enabling electric commercial aircraft, but suffer from material degradation issues that quantum simulation can diagnose) and discovering new catalysts for clean chemical synthesis.

segments.heading: Google's six-milestone roadmap and error correction progress
segments.text: Google Quantum AI tracks progress against a six-milestone roadmap toward a useful fault-tolerant machine. Milestone 1 (quantum supremacy benchmark) was achieved in 2019. Milestone 2 (demonstrating that quantum error correction works in physical hardware) was reached in 2022, when scaling physical qubits to logical qubits produced a modest error reduction. With the Willow chip in 2024, error suppression improved by a factor of 2 below threshold. The team is currently working on Milestone 3: building a high-fidelity logical qubit module that can serve as the scalable building block for modular quantum architectures.

segments.heading: Quantum Echoes: first practical quantum machine learning algorithm
segments.text: While earlier milestones used random circuit sampling as synthetic benchmarks, Quantum Echoes represents a practical quantum algorithm demonstrating real utility. Developed with UC Berkeley researchers, Quantum Echoes extracts structural information from nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) data. In a chemistry demonstration, the algorithm computed the unknown relative dihedral angle between the two benzene rings of diphenyl, solving an open structural question in chemistry using experimental quantum hardware.

segments.heading: Bidirectional acceleration: Quantum plus AI equals Quantum AI
segments.text: Neven and Manyika describe bidirectional synergy between AI and quantum computing. In one direction, AI accelerates quantum engineering: Google DeepMind developed AlphaQubit, applying machine learning decoders to dramatically improve real-time quantum error correction. In the other direction, quantum processors will generate high-value synthetic training datasets for foundation models in molecular biology and materials science, where empirical data collection takes decades (such as the 50 years required to compile the protein structures that trained AlphaFold). Google Quantum AI recently generated its first materials science datasets for DeepMind.

segments.heading: Fundamental physics discoveries on quantum chips
segments.text: Google's quantum processors serve as experimental laboratories for fundamental physics. Demonstrations include simulating holographic duality (creating a traversable wormhole state in entangled qubits based on the AdS/CFT correspondence), observing non-abelian anyons (braiding quasiparticles whose exchanged states alter the global system wave function), and creating time crystals (out-of-equilibrium quantum systems exhibiting perpetual periodic motion without absorbing or dissipating energy).

segments.heading: Post-quantum cryptography timelines moving forward
segments.text: Algorithmic breakthroughs by Google researcher Craig Gidney have drastically reduced the physical qubit count required to break classical public-key cryptography. Breaking RSA-2048 was previously thought to require 20 million physical qubits; Gidney showed it requires roughly 1 million. For elliptic curve cryptography (ECC-256), used widely in digital signatures and blockchain networks, the threshold has dropped to a few hundred thousand qubits. Because of these algorithmic efficiencies, a commercially impactful quantum computer requires roughly 100,000 qubits rather than 1 million (Milestone 5 is the new Milestone 6). Google has urged organizations to transition to post-quantum cryptography standards by 2029.

segments.heading: Quantum noise in generative media and neutral atom architectures
segments.text:
Google Quantum AI has explored feeding quantum probability distributions and noise tensors into diffusion models to generate visual art. Collaborations with digital artist Refik Anadol (Quantum Memories, viewed by 1.3 million museum visitors) and exhibitions in Berlin demonstrated public engagement with quantum-generated media.

In hardware development, Google has opened a second research thread in Boulder, Colorado, investigating neutral atom quantum computing alongside superconducting circuits. While superconducting qubits offer superior gate speed, neutral atom architectures offer natural integration with quantum sensing, which could enable unprecedented precision in physical measurements.

title: Digital health with Dr. Oliver Aalami
description: Discover the fascinating world of digital health innovation with a leading expert in vascular surgery and digital health innovation, Dr. Oliver Aalami. In this insightful People of AI episode, Dr. Aalami shares his path to medicine, his passion for integrating technology in patient care, and his role as director of Stanford's Biodesign for Digital Health program. Explore the groundbreaking projects and initiatives shaping the future of healthcare.

segments.heading: Clinical vascular surgery and the origins of Stanford Biodesign
segments.text: Dr. Oliver Aalami (Vascular Surgeon at Stanford University and Palo Alto VA, and Director of Stanford Biodesign for Digital Health) shares his journey from molecular biology to vascular surgery and digital innovation. The Stanford Biodesign methodology was created to de-risk medical technology through rigorous needs-finding: observing clinical environments as a fly on the wall, identifying unaddressed stakeholder needs, and formulating strict need criteria before designing hardware or software solutions.

segments.heading: Needs finding beyond hospital walls: remote chronic disease management
segments.text: Digital health expands traditional needs-finding beyond inpatient clinics into patients' homes. Aalami explains how sensor-based connected devices (smart scales, blood pressure cuffs, continuous Holter monitors like the Zio Patch) transform chronic disease management by shifting continuous physiological monitoring and behavioral intervention into home settings.

segments.heading: Spezi: open-source modular infrastructure for mobile health research
segments.text: To eliminate redundant mobile app development in academic medical research, Stanford Biodesign created Spezi (formerly CardinalKit). Spezi provides an open-source, modular framework for iOS and Android supporting Bluetooth sensor connectivity, automated onboarding surveys, serverless Firebase backends, Google Colab telemetry analysis pipelines, and native adherence to the HL7 FHIR medical data standard.

segments.heading: The 21st Century Cures Act: democratizing patient electronic health records
segments.text: Aalami highlights underutilized federal mandates under the 21st Century Cures Act requiring electronic health record systems (such as Epic) to expose standardized APIs for patient data access. By leveraging platforms like Android Health Connect, patients can securely sync their comprehensive health records locally onto mobile devices, enabling private on-device intelligence without cloud privacy risks.

segments.heading: LLM on FHIR: conversational clinical records and patient discharge synthesis
segments.text: Stanford researchers developed applications like HealthGPT and LLM on FHIR to turn static, opaque medical records into interactive patient dialogues. For complex post-operative discharge notes or ambiguous lab results (such as thyroid hormone panels), conversational models summarize technical jargon into 5th-grade reading levels, reducing patient anxiety while maintaining clinical accuracy.

segments.heading: Incentive alignment: value-based care, Medicare Advantage, and cross-functional teams
segments.text: Aalami discusses economic adoption models for digital health. While fee-for-service systems incentivize billable procedural interventions, value-based healthcare models (such as Medicare Advantage, Kaiser Permanente, and self-insured employers like Google) financially reward proactive prevention. He emphasizes the necessity of interdisciplinary training, blending clinical medicine with computer science to accelerate real-world clinical translation.

title: Orchestrate generative AI with Workflows
description: Explores orchestrating generative AI pipelines using Google Cloud Workflows. Covers the advantages of serverless workflow orchestration (declarative YAML, automatic retries, state management, parallel branching) over custom glue code. Demos an event-driven map-reduce summarization pipeline triggered by Eventarc that splits long text files in Cloud Storage and parallelizes Vertex AI PaLM/Gemini calls.

segments.heading: Why orchestrate generative AI with Google Cloud Workflows
segments.text: Calling LLM APIs directly from application code introduces fragility: handling network rate limits, managing token quotas, and orchestrating multi-step prompt sequences requires complex retry and error-handling logic. Google Cloud Workflows provides a fully managed, serverless orchestration engine defined in YAML/JSON that handles state persistence, exponential backoff retries, and step execution out of the box.

segments.heading: Calling Vertex AI foundation models from Workflows
segments.text: Workflows includes built-in Google Cloud connectors that call Vertex AI APIs directly using IAM authentication without managing API keys. Developers configure model parameters (temperature, top_p, maxOutputTokens) and parse JSON response candidates natively within workflow expressions.

segments.heading: Event-driven map-reduce summarization with Eventarc and Cloud Storage
segments.text: Mete Atamel demonstrates an end-to-end event-driven architecture: uploading a large text document to Cloud Storage fires an Eventarc event triggering a workflow. The workflow chunks the text, executes parallel workflow branches to summarize individual chapters with Vertex AI simultaneously (Map step), and aggregates the intermediate summaries into a final coherent executive summary (Reduce step).

segments.heading: AI-assisted workflow authoring and future capabilities
segments.text: The session highlights how generative AI assists in writing workflow orchestration definitions themselves, translating natural language business process descriptions into verified Workflows YAML templates.

title: Beyond the hype: Orchestrating end-to-end developer workflows with agents
description: Cloud Next 2026 developer spotlight session addressing the DORA report finding that unmanaged AI tools increase organizational instability. Demonstrates replacing fragmented coding assistants with agent-first developer workflows using Gemini CLI and Antigravity. Features live demos of full-lifecycle issue triage, automated code refactoring, CI/CD verification, and cross-functional collaboration.

segments.heading: The DORA paradox: individual productivity vs. organizational instability
segments.text: The latest DORA report reveals that while 80% of developers report higher individual output using AI coding assistants, organizations suffer increased delivery instability and technical debt when AI is deployed as unstructured copy-paste snippets. Agent-first development solves this by moving from isolated autocomplete to structured, verifiable end-to-end agentic workflows.

segments.heading: Breaking down functional silos between product, design, and engineering
segments.text: Agentic tooling dissolves rigid departmental boundaries. Product managers spin up functional prototypes, designers export live React code connected to real databases, and developers orchestrate backend APIs and infrastructure without endless Jira ticket handoffs.

segments.heading: Live demo: end-to-end issue triage and remediation with Antigravity and Gemini CLI
segments.text: The team demonstrates Antigravity and Gemini CLI resolving a live customer issue: an agent ingests a bug report, traces runtime logs, navigates repository files, plans a minimal reproduction test, modifies code across multiple files, and runs unit tests in an isolated sandbox before submitting a clean pull request.

segments.heading: Enterprise governance, reproducible builds, and developer trust
segments.text: Scaling agentic development requires enterprise guardrails: verifiable test runs, immutable audit trails, and human-in-the-loop review gates. When agents adhere to established CI/CD pipelines, teams maintain software stability while accelerating feature velocity.

title: Building human-centered AI products with Ovetta Sampson
description: Meet Ovetta Sampson, Director of UX for AI compute enablement at Google. She shares her unique path from journalism to AI, including her work on groundbreaking projects prioritizing human-centered design principles. Discover valuable insights into making AI more accessible, the importance of responsible development, and more in this episode of People of AI.

segments.heading: From investigative journalism to machine learning design
segments.text: Ovetta Sampson (Director of UX for AI Compute Enablement at Google) recounts her journey from early computer programming (Commodore 64 at age nine) to 22 years in print and broadcast journalism. Performing computer-assisted reporting on crime and education led her to write SQL, R, and Python models to analyze large public datasets. After earning a master's in human-computer interaction at DePaul University, she joined IDEO in 2016 as an embedded design researcher shaping early machine learning systems with DataScope.

segments.heading: Human-centered AI: augmenting human expertise vs. tech-driven capability
segments.text: Sampson distinguishes between technology-driven development (fitting use cases to raw model capabilities) and human-centered design (solving real human problems by augmenting human cognitive strengths). In an IDEO project designing predictive models for medical malpractice risk, her team interviewed experienced legal intake coordinators-the human algorithms whose 20 years of tacit heuristic pattern recognition formed the qualitative ground truth for the algorithmic features.

segments.heading: Sensor fusion and human problem solving: the AI nose case study
segments.text: Sampson illustrates problem-matching through an edge AI example. Benjamin Cabé initially paired gas sensors with a microcontroller ML model to detect optimal sourdough bread proofing via chemical gas signatures (an AI nose). A 13-year-old developer subsequently adapted this exact sensory architecture in a research lab to detect early gas biomarkers of pneumonia in human respiratory systems, demonstrating how general sensor-model pairings can solve life-saving human needs.

segments.heading: The hazard of traumatized datasets and systemic algorithmic bias
segments.text: Sampson cautions against viewing technology as neutral or socially agnostic. Training predictive models on traumatized or historically discriminatory datasets (such as arrest records in Chicago's Strategic Subjects List or legacy credit scoring models) codifies and scales historical injustices. Developers and data scientists must critically inspect training data lineages, examine social context, and establish ethical checks before training deep neural networks.

segments.heading: Shifting responsible AI from individual developers to system infrastructure
segments.text: At Google, Sampson's UX team works directly on ML infrastructure to simplify responsible AI deployment. Rather than placing the entire compliance burden on individual engineers, modern AI infrastructure builds automated guardrails directly into developer platforms: scanning training datasets for demographic skew, flagging biased feature correlations, providing provenance dashboards, and enforcing auditable model governance similar to banking regulatory standards.

segments.heading: AI literacy, media ethics, and designing for human vulnerability
segments.text: Reflecting on real-world weaponization (such as deepfake voice clones used for defamation), Sampson emphasizes that AI safety requires widespread AI literacy. Guided by ISO human-centered design standards, product designers must actively design against cognitive, physical, and psychological harm by bounding model affordances, providing transparent verification pathways, and designing systems that prioritize societal benefit over raw capability.

title: Physical AI: the new era of robotics
description: Join scientific leaders from Google DeepMind and Boston Dynamics as they unpack the seismic leap in embodied AI. This session will examine how machines are moving beyond scripted automation to possess the general-purpose AI and reasoning required to navigate our physical reality.

segments.heading: Why 2026 is a breakthrough year for robotics
segments.text: Kanishka Rao, Head of Robotics at Google DeepMind, identifies the wave of general-purpose AI breakthroughs as the primary driver. A few years ago, Google adapted large vision-language models (VLMs) for robotics by adding a third modality: action, represented as physical tokens alongside vision and language tokens. The result was a vision-language-action (VLA) model that gave robots human-world understanding for free. A demonstration example: the robot, never having seen the object in robotics training data, correctly identified and picked up a dinosaur toy when asked to pick up the extinct animal. The understanding came from the digital AI pretraining, not from robotics-specific data.

segments.heading: Why humanoid robots: the hardware and data arguments
segments.text:
Alberto Rodriguez, Head of Robotics Behavior at Boston Dynamics, gives two arguments for the humanoid form factor:

1. Data scaling: the most practical path to large-scale data collection for robot training is learning from human demonstration. Matching the human body form factor makes that learning most direct and efficient.

2. Hardware capability: two arms enable load balancing and object repositioning that a single arm cannot do. Two legs give access to essentially any place a human can reach, plus the ability to change the robot's shape and orientation to adapt to tight spaces, and to adjust friction with the ground dynamically for faster acceleration and deceleration than wheeled robots.

Rao adds the physical AGI argument: if AGI means a system that can do anything a human can do, the humanoid form factor is the right substrate for testing that claim.

segments.heading: Two training paradigms: simulation for locomotion, teleoperation for dexterity
segments.text:
Robot training currently divides into two buckets:

1. Simulation-based reinforcement learning: works for tasks that can be simulated with high fidelity, primarily whole-body locomotion and balance. Walking, running, dancing, carrying loads, and whole-body dynamics are all trained in simulation with verifiable reward loops, then transferred to the real world. Boston Dynamics leads on this. The new Atlas robot was designed for mass manufacturing (simpler hardware, higher reliability) specifically to enable large-scale deployment and data collection.

2. Real-world data collection through teleoperation: required for dexterity, because the full variety of objects and manipulation tasks in the world cannot be simulated. Human pilots wearing VR headsets see through the robot's cameras and control it to perform tasks, generating physical tokens that the robot learns from. The goal is that the pilot cannot use information the robot would not have, making the demonstration as close to the robot's actual perception as possible.

segments.heading: Why dexterity is the hardest remaining problem
segments.text:
Rao and Rodriguez identify fine manipulation as the central unsolved challenge in robotics. Key reasons:

1. Whole-body locomotion is largely solved: humanoid balance is solved, as are walking, running, and locomotion over varied terrain. Picking up and placing objects in constrained environments also works well today.

2. Dexterity requires skills that are hard to learn: opening a bottle cap requires force feedback that is both difficult to demonstrate (pilots cannot feel what they are doing through the robot) and difficult to simulate (contact mechanics, skin compression, fingertip sensing are hard to model at the required fidelity).

3. Generalization of verbs to objects remains narrow: a robot trained to unscrew something can do it with a few objects, but does not generalize the verb unscrew the way humans do (once learned, applicable to almost any screwing task). Robots have not achieved universal skill transfer.

Rao notes: today, AI can code an operating system in 24 hours or solve advanced math, but cannot scramble eggs. The gap between digital and physical intelligence is real and distinct.

segments.heading: Vision-based models and the tactile gap
segments.text:
All state-of-the-art robot manipulation models are currently vision-based rather than tactile-based. This is counterintuitive because humans use tactile feedback for most daily manipulation more than vision. Reasons for the current state:

1. Pre-training data: internet-scale vision data is orders of magnitude larger than any tactile dataset.
2. Wrist cameras as tactile proxies: cameras on robot wrists or end effectors provide close-up views of contact points, allowing the model to infer forces from pixel-level compression signals rather than feeling them directly. An origami-folding task (which intuitively requires touch) was successfully demonstrated by a purely vision-based model reading creases and folds.

Rodriguez notes an empirical observation that informs this: humans doing everyday tasks rarely look at their hands while performing them. Eye-tracking studies show that most manipulation is driven by tactile and proprioceptive feedback with only brief visual confirmation. His hypothesis: once reliable tactile hardware exists, robots will shift to using vision primarily for common sense understanding and tactile sensing for high-frequency control loops, mirroring the human architecture.

segments.heading: Thinking tokens in the Gemini robotics model
segments.text:
Google DeepMind introduced thinking tokens in the Gemini robotics model as a mechanism for moving from purely reactive muscle-memory-style action generation to interpretable and steerable behavior.

In standard VLA models, the robot observes an image and outputs an action with no intermediate reasoning. The model cannot explain why it took an action.

With thinking tokens, before generating an action token, the model explicitly generates a text-format reasoning trace about what it is doing and why. Example: I am close enough to close my hand and will grasp the bottle vs. I am not close enough, I need to go lower. The action that follows is conditioned on that thought trace.

Editing the thought trace changes the resulting action in predictable ways, making the model both more interpretable and more steerable. The demonstration from the laundry sorting video showed the model generating thoughts like adjust the black bin a little bit so I can pick up the cloth, a behavior not explicitly present in training, emerging from the combined thinking-and-action training.

segments.heading: Robotics roadmap: timeline and remaining blockers
segments.text:
Rao's timeline estimate: 5 to 10 years before robots capable of general household tasks become realistic. Near-term industrial applications are the earlier entry point.

Remaining technical blockers:
- Dexterity and generalization of manipulation skills to arbitrary objects
- Tactile hardware: current sensors are not reliable or sensitive enough at scale
- Safety: robots are useless without robust safety AI. Rao compares this to autonomous driving, where safety is not a side consideration but an essential requirement before deployment.

Alberto Rodriguez's focus at Boston Dynamics: architecture for multi-frequency decision making. Robots must make some decisions at 1 Hz or less (what object to interact with, what preshape of the hand to use) and others at 50-100 Hz (contact accommodation, balance). The right architecture accommodates both decision frequencies simultaneously. The open research question is what combination of demonstration and trial-and-error training populates this architecture most effectively.

segments.heading: What robots are very good at today
segments.text:
Rao and Rodriguez list current robot capabilities:

- Whole-body balance and locomotion: solved, enabling humanoid robots to walk, run, and navigate stairs
- Pick and place: basic object grasping and placement works well with imitation learning
- Physical tasks in structured environments: Atlas lifts and carries heavy objects (fridge, up to 60 lb boxes via Stretch)
- Inspection and monitoring: Spot patrols industrial facilities on regular schedules, monitoring hundreds or thousands of inspection points reliably, without fatigue or attention drift
- Simulation-based locomotion training: reinforcement learning in simulation with transfer to the real world is working

Industrial challenges still in progress: cable handling (deformable objects with routing requirements), power tool use (requires grip strength calibration), bin picking of single objects from unstructured bins.

segments.heading: Vision for robotics in 10 years
segments.text:
Rao: if dexterity and safety are solved, robots capable of general daily-life tasks (household chores, repetitive and dull work) become realistic within 10 years. The goal is robots handling boring, repetitive, and dangerous physical labor so humans do not have to.

Rodriguez: the target is eliminating arduous physical labor. Stretch already eliminates the need for humans to unload boxes from trucks in 100-degree trailers. Spot eliminates the need for humans to do 500 consecutive identical inspections to catch the 1 anomaly. Atlas targets heavier industrial labor. The commercial roadmap runs from controlled industrial environments (where safety constraints are easier to implement) toward eventually residential and consumer deployments as the technology and safety approaches mature.

title: Beyond the prompt: Build production-ready agents with Google's MCP servers
description: Explores Google's over 50 fully managed remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for services like BigQuery, Cloud Run, GKE, Google Drive, and Gmail. Covers enterprise governance with IAM allow and deny policies, VPCSC, Model Armor content scanning to prevent prompt injection and PII leaks, and Cloud audit logs. Includes a customer case study and architecture walkthrough from Insta360 for an AI video editing agent (Moments Pro).

segments.heading: Connectivity as the bottleneck and the launch of Google-managed MCP servers
segments.text: Experts project over 1 billion deployed agents by 2029, but agents are limited by their connectivity to enterprise systems. Current bottlenecks include non-standardized integrations, inconsistent security per service, and brittle custom connections. While local MCP servers (stdio) work for demos, production enterprises face scale, performance, and compliance hurdles. Google announced over 50 fully managed remote MCP servers across GA and Preview. Every Google Cloud service is now MCP-enabled by default, supporting standardized discovery via Agent Registry, OTel tracing, Cloud audit logs, and Model Armor content scanning.

segments.heading: Demo: Gemini CLI extensions and BigQuery MCP server discovery
segments.text: Google-managed MCP servers are packaged as Gemini CLI extensions for one-click installation. A developer copies the extension URL from Agent Registry and runs gemini mcp install. The CLI uses local Application Default Credentials (ADC) to authenticate via OAuth 2.1 compliant flows. The agent dynamically lists datasets, queries table schemas to understand column structure, and writes and executes SQL queries (for example, identifying top customers by lifetime value) without manual schema hardcoding.

segments.heading: Enterprise governance: IAM policies, IAM Deny, VPCSC, and Model Armor
segments.text: Access to Google-managed MCP servers requires two-layer authorization: underlying API permissions and the specific MCP tool user role. Security administrators can apply granular IAM Deny policies using conditional attributes such as read-only enforcement, blocking specific OAuth client IDs, or denying all MCP access organization-wide. Model Armor provides native content filtering: switching from inspect-only to inspect-and-block automatically redacts or blocks sensitive PII (such as credit card numbers) and protects against prompt injection before data reaches the model. Full end-to-end observability is maintained across MCP calls and underlying API endpoints in Cloud audit logs.

segments.heading: Insta360 case study: Moments Pro AI video editing agent
segments.text: Insta360 (the world's leading 360-degree camera brand with over 6 million creators) built Moments Pro, a conversational video editing assistant powered by Gemini 3. Users describe desired video edits in natural language (for example, 'make a skiing highlight reel'). The orchestrator agent decomposes requests into multi-step editing plans, while specialized sub-agents call Google Cloud tools (upload_to_gcs, query_vector_search, deploy_to_cloudrun, and ffmpeg). Migrating from local tool connections to Google-managed remote MCP servers decoupled the architecture, eliminated infrastructure management (zero-ops), and provided enterprise security across millions of global creators.

title: How to Build a production-ready RAG AI agent
description: Episode 2 of the Hands On AI knowledge base series. Builds an end-to-end production RAG system on Google Cloud: setting up Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL with pgvector, running containerized Apache Beam pipelines on Dataflow to generate text embeddings with Gemini, creating a semantic retrieval layer, wrapping retrieval into an ADK agent, and deploying to Cloud Run.

segments.heading: Hands-on project overview: from structured data to RAG agent
segments.text: Building upon the BigQuery knowledge base from Episode 1, this session constructs a production RAG pipeline. The architecture ingests normalized monster and battle entities, computes high-dimensional vector embeddings, indexes them in Cloud SQL pgvector, and exposes semantic query tools to an ADK agent running on Cloud Run.

segments.heading: Configuring Cloud SQL with pgvector for semantic search
segments.text: The lab provisions a Cloud SQL PostgreSQL instance, enables the pgvector extension, and defines tables storing text payloads alongside 768-dimensional embedding vectors. An HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) index is created to accelerate approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) similarity lookups under high query volume.

segments.heading: Batch embedding generation with Apache Beam and Dataflow
segments.text: To vectorize enterprise datasets efficiently without API throttling, developers deploy a containerized Apache Beam pipeline onto Google Cloud Dataflow. The pipeline reads normalized records, invokes the Gemini text embedding API in parallel batches, and writes vector embeddings directly into Cloud SQL.

segments.heading: ADK RAG agent integration and Cloud Run deployment
segments.text: An Agent Development Kit (ADK) agent is implemented with specialized semantic search tools querying pgvector via cosine similarity. The agent synthesizes retrieved context to answer user inquiries accurately. The service is containerized and deployed to Cloud Run with least-privilege IAM and connection pooling.

title: Fireside chat on an agentic simulation: Race Condition
description: Join Casey West and Tom Greenaway as they chat through some of the development choices and learnings made during the creation of Race Condition. A high-scale agentic AI-powered simulation sandbox with Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

segments.heading: Race Condition overview: reference architecture for agentic simulations
segments.text: Tom Greenaway (Frontend/Gaming Lead) and Casey West (Backend Architect) introduce Race Condition, an open-source reference architecture demonstrating large-scale agentic simulation for planning a marathon along the Las Vegas Strip. Developed for the Google Cloud Next developer keynote, the project showcases the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, combining cloud infrastructure, open standards, and multi-agent coordination.

segments.heading: Core components of an agent: model, instructions, and tools
segments.text: Casey West outlines the foundational structure of an agent within the Agent Development Kit (ADK): an LLM generating actions and narratives, structured instructions defining boundaries and goals, and tools connecting to external services. In Race Condition, specialized agents include Planner agents (designing marathon routes and assessing city traffic/safety impacts), Simulator agents (managing execution loops), and Runner agents (simulating individual participant behavior).

segments.heading: Multi-agent communication: A2A protocol, Agent Cards, and Message Bus
segments.text: The simulation implements Google's Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol. Deployed agents publish structured Agent Cards to the Agent Registry, advertising their capabilities and skills. For high-throughput internal communication between thousands of entities, the architecture avoids point-to-point HTTP bottlenecking by integrating an enterprise message bus using Google Cloud Pub/Sub and Cloud Memorystore (managed Redis), streaming state updates directly to the frontend visualization.

segments.heading: Game development patterns in agentic distributed architectures
segments.text: The architecture borrows core multiplayer game patterns. The backend maintains authoritative game-loop state and ticks every 5 to 10 seconds, while the 3D client functions as a lightweight observer. Client-side collision detection (e.g., runners hitting 3D spherical water stations) triggers events back to the backend, updating agent state (replenishment status) asynchronously. Inter-agent messaging supports natural language queries as well as structured JSON payloads.

segments.heading: Hybrid scaling: deterministic agents vs. open-weight Gemma 4 models
segments.text:
To simulate thousands of concurrent runners cost-effectively without token bottlenecks, the team implemented a dual approach:

1. Deterministic ADK runners: LLM-free rule-based agents responding to structured JSON in milliseconds for massive scale.

2. Model-driven Gemma 4 runners: Open-weight Gemma 4 instances hosted on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) using vLLM for high-concurrency private inference. This configuration allows runners to express chaotic emergent behaviors, internal thoughts, and dynamic decisions without paying per-token API costs on proprietary frontier models.

segments.heading: Context management and subagent token optimization
segments.text: Accumulating chat history across long-running simulations leads to escalating token costs and response latency. Race Condition mitigates this through strict context isolation: subagents receive only immediate local task context without unneeded historical tokens. In addition, historical state is compacted into periodic summaries, keeping per-tick token budgets minimal and response times fast.

segments.heading: Enterprise agent security: Agent Gateway, Identity, and MCP permissions
segments.text:
Securing autonomous agents interacting with enterprise infrastructure requires network-layer controls under a shared responsibility model. The architecture enforces:

- Agent Identity: Cryptographically assigning distinct principal identities to each deployed agent.
- Agent Gateway: Enforcing network-layer RBAC policies on Model Context Protocol (MCP) server endpoints, ensuring planner agents with read access to municipal data cannot invoke destructive budget modification tools.

title: Sameer Samat on Android 17 and the Future of Intelligent Computing
description: Sameer Samat, President of Android at Google, joins host Logan Kilpatrick to discuss Android 17 and what it means to shift from operating systems to intelligence systems. Their conversation covers why Android didn't say the word AI once at the Android Show, the new Gemini Intelligence feature suite including Rambler, app automation, Superfill, and generative widgets, and what it looks like when Gemini can see the road with you in a live demo inside a Volvo EX60.

segments.heading: Why the Android Show never used the word AI
segments.text:
Logan Kilpatrick opens on the difficulty of the job the Android team has: bringing this technology to literally billions of people. He notes that Sameer Samat did not say the word AI once during the Android Show, and that the ecosystem is currently focused on the technology rather than on what it does for the real people using the devices.

Samat frames it as knowing your audience. The Android Show audience is largely people using devices who are excited about technology and want the product they already use to get better. Some are deep on AI, but many are not, because it is a much wider audience. Something is going on with the word AI itself: there is a reaction to it, it is scary for some people, it means different things to different people, and it has become overloaded. Inside Google, and among technologists generally, it is understood as a huge moment and a platform shift that changes everything. But from a consumer standpoint the lesson they have learned is not to lead with the tech, and instead to lead with the benefit.

The feature that taught them this was Circle to Search, launched a couple of years earlier. The concept is simple: hold down the Home button on an Android phone, the screen lights up, and you can circle any object on the screen. It might be the tie someone is wearing that you are interested in, or the lake in a photo on a social media post. Then you ask a question about it: where do I buy that, how do I get there, what is that thing. It worked because these things were genuinely hard to describe to Google before. Samat's point is that if you could describe the tie or the lake well enough to search for it, you would probably already know what it was.

The feature took off. There is a great deal of AI and machine vision behind it, but none of that was mentioned in how it was presented. They showed what you could do with it and people loved it. On other features where they led with the AI, the reception was cooler: people responded with a version of "I don't know about your AI, I'm not feeling that as much." So the show used the word AI zero times even though a lot of the features in it are AI powered, and Samat believes the reception was better that way, because people were being told why something is good and helpful in their life.

segments.heading: Leading with the benefit: on-device scam detection built with DeepMind
segments.text:
Kilpatrick raises the tension in how much AI to lead with, given that everyone is asking who to bet on during a platform shift. His own read is that Android is at the absolute frontier of pushing that shift forward, and he asks how it has actually shown up in the product.

Samat's answer is that the technology matters because it helps build better experiences for the user, and that is fundamentally what drives the team. What the models can do is genuinely wild. There are things Android wanted to do for a long time and could not. He describes seeing mockups of a new feature or concept from a product manager who had not been around long, and having to say that it was not going to work. Now his response is to bring all of those back, because he thinks the tech is ready for them.

His concrete example is scam and spam protection. Android is very popular in a number of countries where the rate of scam and spam is high, which means a lot of phone calls and text messages trying to get you to part with information you should not share. Working with Google DeepMind, they built an on-device model that, with the user's permission, can listen to a call from an unknown number. They worked with a number of banks to make sure the model understood what a bank would never ask a customer for. Banks have consortiums and associations where they agree on those rules together. If the model hears one of those prohibited requests during the call, a warning pops up and the phone vibrates to say that this is a scam and you should hang up right now.

Samat considers that the promise of the technology, and something that affects a very large number of people positively. It is a big part of Android's strategy, but the way to describe it to people is in terms of what it does for you. Kilpatrick adds that Demis Hassabis makes the same point in these planning conversations: technology that works for you. The tension is that Google also wants to say it is at the lead and at the frontier, and those two messages pull against each other.

segments.heading: Balancing on-device models across flagship and entry-level devices
segments.text:
Kilpatrick notes that the scam detection model runs on device, and that a set of recent events made on-device models legible to a lot of people at once: the OpenClaw moment, the release of Gemma 4, and people downloading the AI Edge Gallery app and experimenting with it. Many people suddenly understood that on-device models are going to be powerful and capable and will enable new experiences.

He frames Android's specific tension: there are billions of devices, running the models requires high-end new hardware because it is more performant, and there is a whole group of people without high-end devices who would benefit from AI the most. He asks what the open and on-device model strategy looks like from a platform perspective.

Samat agrees the on-device model strategy is evolving right now, because on-device models are becoming seriously impressive and he thinks they are on the cusp of something amazing. Android's mission is to bring the best of computing to everyone in the world: that means high-end devices and the most basic device you can buy.

He describes two distinct innovation motions. The first is at the high end, creating the future using flagship devices, because those have more system resources. Before you know how to optimize, you use all the system resources available and push the boundary of what is possible. The second motion is flowing those capabilities down, which requires a different approach: you take the kernel of what was built at the flagship level, identify the features that are most profound and most interesting, and find ways to run them on less capable devices. Sometimes that means using the server. Sometimes it means creating different specialized on-device models, and working with silicon providers so those models run efficiently within thermal and battery constraints.

Samat says Android has done this effectively over the years and describes the pattern as sinusoidal. Right now the focus is on the flagship side because that is where the innovation is happening. Some features, including scam detection, are already on device and working for people. The next phase is flowing them down over time.

segments.heading: From operating systems to intelligence systems
segments.text:
Kilpatrick asks what the symbiosis between new models and newly unlocked capabilities means at a macro level for Android, and whether the experience five years out, when models are good enough to run well on the hardware most people already own, will be a totally different experience.

Samat takes a step back to frame it. For the last forty-plus years, computing has created systems that put the user in the role of micromanager of the system. First there was a command line interface asking what you would like to do. Then came the graphical user interface with menus and pointing devices. But it is still the user who conceptualizes the goal, breaks that goal down into all the discrete actions required, and then literally clicks through the sub-actions one at a time. That is the micromanager model of computing, and it remains intimidating: people still take classes to learn software.

The opportunity, and how Samat describes the next several years of Android, is to go from operating systems to intelligence systems. In an intelligence system the user articulates goals, and the system's job is managing resources, managing context, and figuring out how to turn those goals plus the surrounding context into the actions the user wants. Android plans to get this right on flagship devices first. Over time he expects the interface itself to change and become more intent-to-action oriented rather than micromanagement oriented.

segments.heading: Rambler: rebuilding the keyboard around voice, with a live demo
segments.text:
Kilpatrick asks how this changes in the shorter term, and how much voice, which has taken off as a new interface, shows up in the new experiences.

Samat notes that people tend to jump straight to agents when he talks about intent to action, and that agents matter, but he is glad voice came up because input method is one of the fundamental parts of an operating system: how does the user tell the system what they want done. A big part of that is the keyboard, whether on the phone or physical, and it has not changed much in a long time. The last big addition was autocomplete, which he dates to roughly 2012, or possibly 2013 or 2014. Swipe was another addition. Kilpatrick notes he is still fighting autocomplete daily, and Samat agrees it could be a lot better.

Samat calls the keyboard the perfect example of a micromanagement input system: you think about what you want to say, work out the goal of what you are trying to say, break it into the specific words you want to use, and then peck out the letters of those words. It is so habitual that nobody thinks about it.

The feature they announced to change this is called Rambler, rolling out in summer 2026. When you tap the microphone you simply ramble. Instead of faithfully transcribing exactly what you said in dictation form, Rambler takes everything you said and distills it down to what you actually wanted to say, shows it to you for confirmation, and then you send it. Samat connects this to an existing human habit: giving someone a brain dump of your ideas is productive, because verbalizing surfaces things, and the other person reflects back what was interesting. Rambler is the machine equivalent.

The live demo runs inside Google Messages, using the microphone in Google Keyboard, which Samat notes is used hundreds of millions of times a day for voice dictation. He rambles: "Hey there, if you're going to the store, can you pick up some fruit? Maybe like some bananas, mangoes, strawberries, and oranges. Actually, never mind the bananas. We don't need any more of those. We have plenty of those." The result contains none of the hesitation sounds, and the self-correction about bananas is resolved rather than transcribed: the model understands the bananas are not wanted. He then asks it to turn the text into a list and to add some emoji, and it does both.

Kilpatrick asks whether it runs on device. Samat says no, this is currently talking to the server, and they have made it very fast. A deliberate tuning decision: they did not want the output to read in a style people associate with a chatbot, so it is tuned for a more conversational tone. That is why it did not produce a list initially and had to be asked. Samat calls the added emoji gratuitous but did it anyway.

Rambler works for simple texts and equally well for dictating something longer like a paper. It will be a mode you can use the microphone in, and typing on the keyboard remains available. Samat presents it as a major upgrade to the keyboard and a large part of what they mean by an intelligent system: the keyboard itself is now intelligent.

segments.heading: App Automation and Android's virtual window system
segments.text:
Kilpatrick frames input as the first step of the transformation and actions taken on the device as the second: Android going and clicking things in the phone, so the user articulates intent in voice and Android does the micromanaging.

Samat confirms this is the feature they call App Automation, and it is exactly what it sounds like: you tell Gemini you want to get something done. Kilpatrick points out that App Automation is the ideal illustration of the naming principle, because the name sells the outcome, automating apps on your phone, rather than the AI.

When shown to people, the reaction is a mix of being impressed and being a little nervous, so the team worked to make it approachable. The main mechanism is a virtual window system built into Android.

Samat grounds it in his preferred example, chosen because it has real complexity. He has a list of people coming to his barbecue on screen, and each person in the list has the size of their party and whether they are vegetarian. He long-presses the power button, which brings up screen context for Gemini so it can see the document with him, and asks Gemini to go to Instacart and put what he will need for the barbecue for all these people into his cart at Safeway.

When Gemini starts Automation, it opens the task in a virtual window: a containerized environment where the designated app and Gemini both exist, and which the user can minimize into the status bar and return to at any time. The AI agent cannot go outside that container, which means it cannot use other apps. The user can watch it work, and Samat says it is sometimes fun to watch, because the model's thinking appears at the bottom of the screen as it goes.

In his run of the barbecue example, the agent navigated through Safeway and independently arrived at the observation that hot dog buns and hot dogs never come in matching package counts. Its visible reasoning worked through needing more buns than hot dogs and how to resolve that. It also worked out that veggie burgers were needed, added everything to the cart, and then sent a notification saying the cart was ready for review.

A deliberate safety boundary: Automation stops before completing transactions. Samat says building trust with the consumer and having that safety around it matters right now, so the agent hands back and the user pushes the commit button themselves. The time saving is the proposition.

Kilpatrick asks whether containerized apps running on the phone existed before. Samat says Android has always had an app container and a per-app isolation layer, but the notion of something else driving the screen while confined to that container, inside a minimizable virtual window, is new. There was no need for it before, because these are single-user systems where the user is on the device doing their own thing, and a headless process generating UI in the background served no purpose. The model does need it, because it has to look at and see what is on the screen.

On the longer term, Samat sees three approaches converging under the agent: MCP integrations, Chrome doing a form of auto browse to manage and complete things, and this screen-driving approach. The user tells Gemini what they want done and Gemini decides which of these tools is best.

Asked whether Automation is vision-based, Samat confirms it is: Gemini looks at the screen and chooses coordinates to tap, using the app just as a person would. It decides to open a menu, opens it, taps the search bar, and starts searching for hot dog buns. The intended user model is handing your phone to a trusted assistant and asking them to get something done for you.

segments.heading: Gemini Intelligence and Superfill: never fill out a form again
segments.text:
Kilpatrick asks about Gemini Intelligence, which is what kicks off the Automation workflow, for anyone who missed the headline.

Samat explains they wanted a way to describe the best Gemini experience, and Gemini Intelligence is that name. It was announced at the Android Show a couple of weeks before this conversation, and it covers a set of capabilities at the bleeding edge. Rambler and Automation are part of it.

The capability he is most enthusiastic about is Superfill. His motivation is personal and blunt: he wants to get rid of forms and never fill one out again. After booking a set of flights for a summer vacation he has his fifteen-year-old's passport number memorized, which he does not want to have memorized. Kilpatrick notes he does not even know his own passport number.

Superfill extends a familiar idea. Autofill already works for your name, your address, and possibly your credit card information. Superfill is that, extended to many other fields. If you have given Gemini permission, which Samat stresses is an important step, it can pull information that already exists in your Google account and suggest it in real time as you fill out a form: a passport uploaded to Google Photos, a confirmation code sitting in an email.

Kilpatrick asks about the mechanism. Does the model notice an open form field and try to retrieve something plausible, or is there a fixed set of categories it pulls into personal context? Samat says that initially, to get the precision and recall trade-off right and to make sure users become comfortable enough to rely on it, they have limited it to a set of entity types: passport information, driver's licenses, and vehicle license plates.

His favorite case is the license plate. The DMV registration is sitting in your email. You park somewhere, scan the QR code in the parking lot, and the parking app asks for your car's license plate while you are already walking out of the lot, which normally sends you searching through Photos or Gmail. With Superfill it is offered to you directly.

The implementation: a system has already retrieved those entities and holds them pre-prepared in a centralized repository. When the on-device system detects that you are looking at a form needing one of those entities, it makes a secure request to pull that information and presents it in the keyboard, asking whether you want to autofill it. If you accept, it grabs the value and puts it in the field. Samat says all of this is coming in summer 2026.

As an aside, Kilpatrick lobbies for renaming Rambler to something built on the word Yap, suggesting Yap Mode, on the grounds that people love to yap. Samat says it is a good point and he would have to check whether it is trademarkable.

segments.heading: Generative widgets and the beginning of generative UI in the OS
segments.text:
The last Gemini Intelligence capability Samat covers is generative widgets, which he thinks speaks to how UI may evolve.

Widgets are the ultimate form of customization on Android and have long been a loved way to customize the home screen, but someone has to build the widget for you first. The generative widget concept removes that dependency: you tell Gemini what you want to see, for example the latest lap times for yesterday's F1 race, and ask it to keep that updated and build you the widget. Nobody may have built that particular widget. Gemini works on it for a while and produces exactly that widget, pulling from publicly available sources of information.

Samat calls this the beginning of generative UI for your operating system, and expects the pattern to expand over time so that more of the UI is built for you on the fly.

segments.heading: Does the agentic shift kill apps: experiential versus transactional
segments.text:
Kilpatrick recalls the line that Android is the platform for builders, and notes everything discussed so far delivers on it. He then raises a question he likes to ask inside Google: will Google in five years have ten thousand products or three products, ten thousand apps or three apps. His point is that Android, as an operating system whose predominant interface is showing up and going through apps, faces interesting implications. More people are building apps than ever before, while at the same time everyone appears to be trying to build super apps.

Samat calls it a genuinely interesting moment, because there is talk that there will be no reason for apps at the same time as a wave of first-time developers is being created.

He does not think apps go away. He relates it to what people call the SaaS-pocalypse, where SaaS companies were hit hard on the theory that agentic AI removes the need for those applications: users will either make their own or the existing products lose their UIs and become commoditized backends. Samat considers that a surface-deep way of looking at what will actually happen, because not all SaaS is the same. Applying the same shallow reasoning to what he calls the app-pocalypse requires going deeper.

Part of going deeper is understanding consumer behavior. Looking at what consumers actually do on their phones, they spend seventy to eighty plus percent of their time in apps he would call experiential: TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, chatting with friends, playing games. That is the bulk of time spent. Apps that are more transactional in nature, such as booking a ride or getting a meal, account for some of the time, but less than you would expect. Less time spent does not mean less important.

He suggests plotting apps on a two-by-two, one axis being how experiential an app is and the other how transactional, since apps can sit in the middle. Time clusters on the experiential, less transactional side.

From this he concludes the grid of apps will evolve, but he does not think anyone wants their agent watching TikTok or YouTube for them. Users still want to kick back and do some of that themselves, engage with friends on messaging, and play their games. The transactional apps are the ones that will change most, and he expects those to end up with two modes: an experiential version offering a much richer, more engaging experience, and a mode where the app is almost agentic itself, responding to agentic queries from others.

His example is Google Maps, with the caveat that he does not run the Maps team. Maps has an Ask Maps feature, which he reads as its agentic mode of being. Planning an event, you might ask your agent for great venues around Tahoe. Then, wanting to understand the indoor to outdoor flow of a specific venue, you open Maps yourself, switch to satellite view, zoom in and look around. That second part is the experiential view.

So his conclusion is not that apps go away, but that the transactional side becomes much more nuanced, and that people may end up with more time for experiential apps rather than less.

Kilpatrick draws a parallel to commerce and retail malls, where both ends of the spectrum exist. Buying his mother something at Williams-Sonoma, the staff greeted him warmly and offered him a coffee when he had come in for a spatula, which struck him as deliberately experiential and unlike a normal shopping trip. At the other end, on any of those companies' websites, he is in transaction mode: find the thing, click the fewest buttons, buy it, and leave. Retailers have innovated and changed the way shopping works in store precisely because customers can now transact elsewhere.

Samat adds that easier completion tends to expand overall usage: if something becomes much easier for him to get done, he does more of it. Retail and commerce combined, offline plus online, is larger than it was before. He notes that in every platform shift there is a narrative that the old thing completely goes away, and it usually does not: these things tend to build on each other. The web did not eliminate going to physical locations, and physical experiences are arguably becoming more important. Mobile did not eliminate the desktop. He considers the agentic move huge and profound and does not want to predict that it will not be different, but his expectation is accumulation rather than replacement.

segments.heading: Android Halo: a place in the status bar for long-running agents
segments.text:
The way Android is handling background agent work is a new concept called Android Halo. It is a dedicated location in the status bar where the user's agent of choice, Gemini or another agent, can post updates and take input on the task or tasks it is running.

The reasoning is that an agent doing work in the background will need to ask the user a question, give an update, or show a result, and the user needs somewhere to follow along. Samat presents Halo as an interesting new spot for how computing may evolve, with the operating system making it more seamless to engage with long-running tasks.

segments.heading: Voice as a native interface across form factors
segments.text:
Before moving to the car demo, Kilpatrick asks about text and voice as interfaces from an Android ecosystem perspective, given that voice is one of the native form factors everyone is used to and text is already how people communicate with each other.

Samat says voice is very natural for a lot of people, and in certain form factors it is the only sensible interface: in the car, with a pair of glasses, or on a run with a watch. In those cases it is genuinely valuable that the machine can now understand natural language, because voice was the only available channel and previously the experience was workable but awkward.

He sees a generational shift. Younger consumers, including his own children, hardly type on their phones at all and constantly use the microphone to speak. Sending voice recordings rather than text is common. Voice is also more efficient: you can typically speak three to five times faster than you can type. His conclusion is that embracing voice, with simple and straightforward ways of using it, unlocks new use cases now that the machine understands you much better.

Kilpatrick notes that places where you previously could not wield intelligence are opening up. You could not do anything useful in a car because you had to focus on driving, and that is changing.

segments.heading: Gemini built into the Volvo EX60: natural language car controls
segments.text:
The demo moves into a Volvo EX60, a vehicle that had not shipped at the time of recording.

The car has Google built-in, meaning Google and Gemini run on the infotainment system powered by Android. Because of that, Android and Gemini have much deeper access to the car's systems.

Samat demonstrates climate control by voice: he says the car is stuffy and asks Gemini to adjust the climate. Gemini responds that it is increasing the fan speed and turning off air recirculation, and makes both adjustments. He points out that he would not normally have the climate menu open while driving, so seeing the changes applied on screen is the confirmation.

The second demonstration is a driver assistance control. Without touching any physical controls he asks Gemini to turn on lane keeping assist, and it confirms that it is turning on the lane keeping aid. Samat highlights the speed and the fact that he can speak in natural language: there is no longer a requirement to say an exact phrase in an exact way, which he attributes to Gemini.

segments.heading: Gemini seeing the road with you: front camera grounding
segments.text:
The second capability wired into this vehicle connects Gemini to the car's front-facing cameras. The intent was to find out what becomes possible if Gemini, with the user's permission, can see the world as you drive through it.

Samat is explicit about the privacy design. Gemini is not watching what you are seeing at all times. The camera feed is provided to Gemini only when you invoke it and ask a question, for a limited period. Gemini answers, and then loses the ability to see again. Asked whether it only sees from the moment of activation onward, Samat says it keeps a local buffer.

Three live queries follow. Asked what it sees around them, Gemini reports that they are at the Googleplex in Mountain View surrounded by lush greenery and modern office buildings, and identifies Google Building 1020 Charleston Road on the left, describing its brick-accented exterior and noting it is part of the extensive Landings office complex.

Driving on, Samat asks about a white sculpture ahead on the right and the building behind it, something he says he had always wondered about and could not describe well enough to look up. Gemini identifies the sculpture as the Orb, a thirty-three-foot-tall public art installation made of over 6,400 aluminum panels that create unique light patterns, and the building behind it as Gradient Canopy, noting its signature dragon-scale solar roof that generates a significant portion of the building's own power. Neither host nor guest knew about the solar roof.

The third query asks about a white tent-like set of buildings on the left. Gemini identifies them as part of the Shoreline Amphitheater, an outdoor music venue known for its distinctive peaked roof design, built on a former landfill, now hosting major concerts and festivals in a scenic park-like setting.

Samat frames the open question as how Gemini seeing along with you can genuinely make life easier, and says the team is still working through how best to launch this in vehicles. Kilpatrick suggests grounding against Street View when you are trying to find the right place to turn and the location looks unfamiliar. Samat adds street signs in a different language, or signs that are simply confusing, as cases where explanation on the spot would help.

title: Scale AI agents in production
description: Covers Google's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform architecture across four pillars: Build, Scale, Govern, and Optimize. Introduces the new Agent CLI with automated scaffolding and eval loops, Agent Runtime with subsecond warm starts and 7-day workflows, Memory Bank, and sandboxes. Features production case studies from Comcast (Xfinity Assistant 2.0 with decoupled session architecture) and Palo Alto Networks (autonomous network remediation with 24% autonomous resolution rate).

segments.heading: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: the four pillars
segments.text: Moving from prototype to production requires a vertically integrated stack across four areas: (1) Build: over 200 foundation models, ADK updates, low-code Agent Studio, and the new Agent CLI; (2) Scale: upgraded Agent Runtime supporting 7-day workflows, subsecond warm starts, bidirectional streaming, managed Sessions, Memory Bank, and isolated Sandboxes (code execution with 14-day TTL and Chromium-based computer use); (3) Govern: fleet management via Agent Identity, Agent Gateway, and Agent Registry for up to 3,000 agents per project; (4) Optimize: simulation, automated evaluation, and trajectory observability.

segments.heading: Demo: Agent CLI lifecycle and automated evaluation loop
segments.text: Prototyping is fast, but production iteration cycles often take weeks. The open-source Agent CLI embeds expert ADK knowledge into coding agents (Antigravity IDE, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Claude Code). A demo building a customer support agent for an online shoe store shows the CLI: (1) clarifying intent and requirements, (2) scaffolding ADK codebase, (3) generating synthetic test datasets and executing automated eval loops with self-correcting code updates until all test criteria pass, (4) one-click deployment to Agent Runtime, and (5) running conversational analysis on production BigQuery telemetry.

segments.heading: Comcast case study: Xfinity Assistant 2.0 and decoupled session management
segments.text: Comcast's Xfinity Assistant serves millions of customers across digital apps and hardware. Transitioning from rigid rule-based trees to generative AI (XA 2.0), Comcast solved a critical operational challenge: agent in-memory sessions were lost during rolling code upgrades, causing active users to lose troubleshooting context. Working with Google Cloud, Comcast decoupled session management into a dedicated session service shared across steering, repair, and technician dispatch agents. Live demos show end-to-end technician scheduling and proactive appointment tracking.

segments.heading: Palo Alto Networks case study: autonomous network reasoning ecosystem
segments.text: Palo Alto Networks replaced static support workflows with an autonomous reasoning multi-agent system powered by Gemini 2.5/3.0 Flash, Bigtable, and Vertex AI Search. A Root Agent handles multimodal user inputs (e.g., server rack photos) and applies guardrails with human off-ramps. A specialized RCA Agent executes dynamic investigation DAGs up to three iterations over logs, metrics, and network configs. Production benchmarks achieved: sub-100 second end-to-end resolution, 2-5 second streaming thought latency, and a 24% autonomous resolution rate.

title: Science in the age of AI
description: Google I/O 2025 science keynote exploring landmark breakthroughs powered by AI across biology, medicine, and physical sciences. Google DeepMind and Google Research leaders discuss AlphaFold 3 and the free AlphaFold Server for molecular modeling, TxGemma open foundation models for therapeutics discovery, AMIE diagnostic dialogue agents with multimodal vision, and neural PDE solvers for climate prediction.

segments.heading: AI driving landmark advances across the scientific frontier
segments.text: James Manyika opens the session highlighting Google's commitment to applying AI to fundamental science. Rather than viewing AI solely as an economic productivity tool, AI models act as catalytic research tools accelerating discovery across structural biology, genomics, materials science, and climate dynamics.

segments.heading: AlphaFold 3 and the AlphaFold Server: modeling the entire biomolecular universe
segments.text: Pushmeet Kohli details AlphaFold 3, which expands beyond single protein structures to model complex interactions across proteins, DNA, RNA, ligands, and chemical modifications in a single unified diffusion architecture. DeepMind offers the AlphaFold Server for free to non-commercial researchers globally, drastically accelerating biological and pharmaceutical research.

segments.heading: Therapeutics and clinical AI: TxGemma and AMIE multimodal diagnostics
segments.text: Joëlle Barral presents TxGemma, an open-weights foundation model suite fine-tuned on biochemical and therapeutic benchmarks. In medical diagnostics, the AMIE agent adds multimodal vision to conversational reasoning, demonstrating clinical diagnostic dialogue and visual symptom reasoning exceeding primary care physician benchmarks in simulated clinical trials.

segments.heading: AI for physical sciences and climate modeling with Anima Anandkumar
segments.text: Caltech Professor Anima Anandkumar discusses using Fourier Neural Operators and physics-informed ML to solve complex partial differential equations (PDEs) up to orders of magnitude faster than numerical solvers, enabling real-time weather forecasting (GraphCast), seismic imaging, and carbon sequestration simulations.

title: Boost AI context with hybrid search in Spanner
description: Explores how Google Cloud Spanner delivers high-relevance AI context via built-in Hybrid Search. Explains combining BM25 full-text keyword indexing with high-dimensional vector embeddings in unified SQL/GQL queries. Highlights Spanner's 99.999% availability SLA, zero-maintenance global scaling, and enterprise use cases in e-commerce, content management, and healthcare.

segments.heading: Spanner as a foundational search and AI data platform
segments.text: Cloud Spanner powers core Google properties (Drive, Gmail, YouTube, Google Photos) and global enterprises like Uber. It combines relational consistency with multi-model search capabilities (full-text search, vector embeddings, and graph traversal) on a single unified dataset with 99.999% availability and limitless horizontal scalability.

segments.heading: The power of Hybrid Search: BM25 keyword matching plus vector similarity
segments.text: Pure vector search can miss exact keywords (part numbers, specific proper nouns, acronyms), while pure keyword search misses semantic synonyms and conceptual intent. Spanner Hybrid Search executes both BM25 token matching and dense vector similarity scoring within a single SQL statement, applying Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) to return maximally grounded context to AI agents.

segments.heading: Enterprise search use cases: e-commerce, healthcare, and content management
segments.text: Real-world implementations illustrate hybrid search advantages: e-commerce platforms match customer queries with fuzzy spelling tolerances and product catalog embeddings; healthcare applications cross-reference doctor specializations with patient clinical histories; content management systems search multi-terabyte document corpuses with near-zero latency.

segments.heading: Integration with Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
segments.text: Spanner integrates directly into the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform via Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and SQL ML extensions, allowing autonomous agents to query live operational data without building external ETL pipelines or maintaining separate vector databases.

title: Boost AI context with hybrid search in Spanner
description: Go beyond keyword search to get the most out of your operational data. In this session, learn to build sophisticated, AI-powered experiences with Spanner. Discover how to combine full-text and vector search into powerful multi-model queries that deeply understand user intent. New AI innovations simplify contextual search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications. Explore seamless integrations with the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform to create the next generation of contextual, intelligent, multi-model search.

segments.heading: Spanner as the underlying search platform for Google products
segments.text: Spanner is the data platform under most Google consumer products, and Spanner Search is used for in-product search in Google Drive, Gmail, YouTube, and Photos. Spanner Search is also offered to Cloud Spanner customers. Uber's search runs on Spanner. Key platform advantages for search workloads: zero maintenance, near-limitless scalability, five-nines SLA, and multi-model architecture (relational, search, and graph workloads can run against the same data without copying it).

segments.heading: Three search modalities: full-text, vector, and hybrid
segments.text: Spanner Search offers three search methods. Full-text search performs keyword-based token matching using an inverted index, with fuzzy search for spelling variants and synonyms. Vector search uses AI embeddings to match based on semantic meaning rather than exact keywords: a search for space LEGO for 8 plus can return results about STEM toy sets that do not contain those words. Hybrid search merges both modalities using techniques like Reciprocal Rank Fusion to produce results that combine precision (from keyword matching) with recall (from semantic matching). Before Spanner, implementing these modalities required running separate platforms and maintaining ETL pipelines between them.

segments.heading: Full-text search deep dive: n-grams, fuzzy search, and intelligent query expansion
segments.text: Spanner full-text search tokenizes columns defined in DDL using SQL. Tokenize_ngrams splits text into size-3 character substrings, creating a fuzzy-matching inverted index. A search for Jennifer matches Jennifer, Jennifer as a substring match, and Jenny as an alternate spelling. The order_by_score function ranks results by text relevance rather than row ID. Enhanced query (intelligent search expansion) is Google's proprietary technology from Google Search: a search term like hair dye is automatically expanded to hair, hair dye, color, coloring, dyeing, and related terms before hitting the index. Atteo (case study) reported a step-change improvement in result quality across multilingual customer data by enabling enhanced query. Also announced at GA: custom dictionaries, allowing domain-specific synonym and expansion mappings to be plugged into the search pipeline.

segments.heading: Vector search in Spanner: KNN, ScaNN, and transactional consistency
segments.text: Spanner supports both KNN (exact nearest neighbor) and ANN (approximate nearest neighbor) vector search. KNN is appropriate for small, filtered result sets (for example, Gmail searches only within a single user's mail). ANN builds a tree-structure clustering index over the full vector space and returns approximate top-K results much faster and cheaper. ScaNN (Scalable Approximate Nearest Neighbors) is Google's proprietary ANN algorithm, the same index behind Google Search and YouTube. Spanner's ANN index is transactionally consistent: when a document is written, its embedding is indexed immediately with no ETL or sync delay. Tested with 10 billion-plus vectors. Vector latency improvements were announced, with significant reductions since six months prior; index build times were also reduced.

segments.heading: Hybrid search templates: vector-ranked full-text and multi-retriever fusion
segments.text: Two main hybrid search patterns in Spanner. Pattern 1: use full-text search as the retriever and vector search for ranking. A WHERE clause does full-text token matching; the ORDER BY uses Euclidean distance on the document embedding versus the query embedding. This brings semantic relevance ranking to keyword-retrieved results in a five-line SQL query. Pattern 2: two retrievers, one full-text and one vector, merged using RRF (Reciprocal Rank Fusion) or relative score functions. The full-text retriever returns precise keyword matches (space-themed products), the vector retriever returns semantically related results (Star Trek, Star Wars toys), and the fusion layer ranks the combined set. Reranking using ML models is also supported.

segments.heading: Graph and GraphRAG in Spanner
segments.text: Spanner Graph is defined as an overlay on existing relational tables: no data copy is needed.
